# Frameworks for Organizing Personal Knowledge ("Tools for Thought")

## Comprehensive List

Below is a broad catalogue of named systems, methods, and philosophies that have emerged from the personal knowledge management (PKM) and "tools for thought" communities. They range from highly prescriptive procedures to lighter philosophical stances.

### Foundational / Historical Methods
| Framework | Origin | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Zettelkasten** | Niklas Luhmann (1960s–90s) | Numbered, atomic, densely linked slip-box notes |
| **Cornell Note-Taking Method** | Walter Pauk (1950s) | Three-zone page layout for capture + recall |
| **SQ3R** | Francis Robinson (1946) | Survey → Question → Read → Recite → Review |
| **Feynman Technique** | Richard Feynman | Explain a concept simply to test understanding |

### Modern PKM Systems
| Framework | Origin | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **PARA** | Tiago Forte (2019) | Sort everything into **P**rojects, **A**reas, **R**esources, **A**rchives |
| **CODE** | Tiago Forte (2019) | **C**apture → **O**rganize → **D**istill → **E**xpress |
| **Building a Second Brain (BASB)** | Tiago Forte, book 2022 | PARA + CODE + Progressive Summarization as one system |
| **Progressive Summarization** | Tiago Forte | Layered re-reading: highlight → bold → annotate → extract |
| **Evergreen Notes** | Andy Matuschak / Nick Milo | Notes written as standalone, citable claims that evolve over time |
| **Maps of Content (MOC)** | Andy Matuschak | Hand-curated index notes that map a topic's territory |
| **Linguistic Organization** | Andy Matuschak | Organize by the *language* you use to describe things, not by folders |
| **Atomic Notes** | Various (Matuschak, Milo, etc.) | One idea per note; link rather than file |
| **The "Tools for Thought" philosophy** | Andy Matuschak (blog, 2020–) | Notes as thinking instruments; prefer linking, naming, and evolving over filing |

### Productivity / Workflow Systems (knowledge-adjacent)
| Framework | Origin | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **GTD (Getting Things Done)** | David Allen (2001) | Capture → Clarify → Organize → Reflect → Engage |
| **DiSCo** | David Allen (2021) | **D**o it, **S**chedule it, **C**ontextualize it, **O**ffload it |
| **The Eisenhower Matrix** | (attributed) | Urgent / Important quadrants for triage |

### Learning-Science Techniques (often layered on top)
| Framework | Origin | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Spaced Repetition** | Ebbinghaus → Anki community | Review at expanding intervals |
| **Active Recall** | Roediger & Karpicke | Test yourself instead of re-reading |
| **Elaborative Interrogation** | Chi et al. | Ask "why is this true?" for every new fact |
| **Interleaving** | Rohrer & Taylor | Mix topics during practice |

### Structural / Technical Approaches
| Framework | Origin | Core Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Knowledge Graphs** | Academic / Semantic Web | Nodes + typed edges; formal ontology of your notes |
| **Tagging vs. Filing** | Community debate | Flat tags (many-to-many) vs. hierarchical folders (one parent) |
| **Backlinking / Bidirectional Links** | Obsidian, Roam, Logseq | Every note sees what points to it |
| **The "Linking" Philosophy** | Zettelkasten + Matuschak | The *links* are the knowledge, not the notes |

---

## Top Three in Detail

### 1. Zettelkasten (Luhmann's Slip-Box)

**What it is.** A method for creating a personal, growing, *linked* body of notes that functions as an external memory and thinking partner. Luhmann, a German sociologist, used it to publish 70+ books and 400+ papers.

**Core procedures:**

1. **Atomic capture.** Each note states *one* idea in your own words. No summaries of whole articles; no multi-topic pages.
2. **Permanent numbering.** Every note gets a unique, hierarchical ID (e.g., `1a`, `1a2`, `1a2b`). The number encodes *where the note was born in a chain of thought*, not a topic category.
3. **Link at creation.** When you write a new note, you *must* link it to at least one existing note and explain the relationship ("this contradicts…", "this is an example of…", "this extends…").
4. **Write to the box, not for the box.** Notes are written for your future self, in complete sentences, so they are understandable without the original source.
5. **No folders, no tags.** Organization emerges from the link structure. You navigate by following threads, not by browsing categories.
6. **Regular review.** Periodically re-read notes; prune, rewrite, or re-link as understanding deepens.

**Best-practice principles:**
- *Write in your own words* — paraphrasing forces comprehension.
- *One idea per card* — if a note has two ideas, split it.
- *The link is the argument* — a link without a stated relationship is noise.
- *Let structure emerge* — resist the urge to pre-organize into categories.

**When it shines:** long-form writing, research, building a personal "theory base." It is the intellectual ancestor of Roam Research, Obsidian, and most modern "networked note" tools.

---

### 2. PARA + CODE — "Building a Second Brain" (Tiago Forte)

**What it is.** The most widely adopted modern PKM system. It splits the problem into two orthogonal axes: **where** things live (PARA) and **what you do** with them (CODE). Forte's 2022 book *Building a Second Brain* packages them together.

**PARA — the organizing structure (the "where"):**

| Bucket | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **P**rojects | "What am I actively working toward a deadline?" | "Launch v2 of the app" |
| **A**reas | "What ongoing responsibilities do I maintain?" | "Health," "Team management" |
| **R**esources | "What topics am I curious about?" | "Behavioral economics," "CSS tricks" |
| **A**rchives | "What's done or dormant?" | Last year's completed projects |

Key rule: sort by **actionability**, not by topic. A note about "sprint planning" goes under the *project* you're doing, not under a "Management" folder.

**CODE — the workflow (the "what"):**

1. **Capture** — Collect anything that sparks interest into an inbox (notes app, bookmark, voice memo). Zero judgment at this stage.
2. **Organize** — File each captured item into a PARA bucket using the *most actionable* category. Use a simple folder hierarchy; avoid deep nesting.
3. **Distill** — Apply **Progressive Summarization**: re-read a note and add layers of emphasis (highlight → bold → inline annotation → extract the key passage into a standalone "evergreen" note). The goal is to make the *most important sentence* the first thing you see.
4. **Express** — Use your notes as raw material for output: a blog post, a talk, a decision, a conversation. Output is the point; the system is a means.

**Best-practice principles:**
- *Actionability over taxonomy* — "Will I use this in the next 30 days?" beats "What subject is this?"
- *Minimal filing effort* — if organizing takes more than 30 seconds, your structure is too complex.
- *Notes are for producing* — a note that is never used in an output is a liability.
- *Progressive Summarization* — don't annotate everything; layer emphasis so future-you can scan in seconds.

**When it shines:** people who drown in bookmarks, PDFs, and "someday" folders. It is deliberately low-philosophy and high-pragmatism.

---

### 3. Evergreen Notes + MOCs + Linguistic Organization (Andy Matuschak's "Tools for Thought")

**What it is.** Not a single rigid system but a *philosophy* for treating notes as instruments of thought rather than storage. Matuschak (a researcher at Meta) articulated it across a widely-read blog series (2020–2023). It is the intellectual bridge between Luhmann's Zettelkasten and modern outliner tools.

**Three interlocking practices:**

**(a) Evergreen Notes**
- A note is written as a **self-contained, citable claim** — a single sentence or short paragraph that would make sense to a stranger.
- Example: *"Cognitive load increases with the number of open loops in working memory."*
- They are **not** summaries, not meeting notes, not clippings. They are *your* distilled understanding.
- They **evolve**: you rewrite them as your understanding sharpens. Version history matters.

**(b) Maps of Content (MOCs)**
- A MOC is a **hand-curated index note** for a topic. It lists the evergreen notes that touch that topic, grouped into sub-themes, with brief annotations explaining *why* each note is there.
- MOCs are **not** folders. A single evergreen note can appear in many MOCs.
- They are the "table of contents" of a thought territory, written in prose, not a flat tag list.
- You create a MOC *after* you've accumulated enough notes to see a structure; you don't pre-build the taxonomy.

**(c) Linguistic Organization**
- Instead of asking "which folder does this go in?", ask **"what words do I use to describe this?"**
- Your vocabulary *is* your taxonomy. If you have a rich, precise vocabulary (e.g., "cognitive load," "sunk cost," "preemptive"), notes organize themselves around those terms.
- This is why Matuschak emphasizes *writing* as the primary organizing act: the act of putting an idea into words forces you to choose the right concept-name, which is the filing step.

**Best-practice principles:**
- *Notes are for thinking, not storing.* If a note isn't helping you reason, it's clutter.
- *Linking > filing.* The value is in the web of connections, not the folder hierarchy.
- *Name things precisely.* Good names (evergreen-note titles, MOC titles) do the work of classification.
- *Let structure emerge.* Resist building elaborate taxonomies before you have the notes to fill them.
- *Revisit and rewrite.* A note you haven't touched in a year is a candidate for deletion or radical rewording.

**When it shines:** researchers, writers, and anyone building a long-term intellectual body of work. It is the most "philosophical" of the three and the least prescriptive about tooling, but the most powerful for deep, cumulative thinking.

---

## How They Relate

```
Zettelkasten (1960s)
   │  atomic notes, linking, no folders
   ▼
Evergreen Notes + MOCs (2020s, Matuschak)
   │  refines "atomic" → "citable claim"; adds MOCs as
   │  emergent indexes; adds linguistic organization
   ▼
PARA + CODE (2019, Forte)
   │  orthogonal axis: actionability-based filing +
   │  progressive summarization for distillation
   ▼
Hybrid in practice
   • PARA for the *outer* structure (projects, areas)
   • Evergreen notes + MOCs for the *inner* knowledge web
   • CODE as the daily workflow that feeds both
```

Most practitioners end up blending elements. The three frameworks above are complementary rather than competing: **Zettelkasten** gives you the linking discipline, **PARA/CODE** gives you a low-friction filing and distillation workflow, and **Evergreen Notes + MOCs** give you the philosophy that makes the whole thing a thinking instrument rather than a filing cabinet.

# Scope and Limitations

## Scope

This study investigates and defines the effectiveness of the alignment guide tool in promoting accurate and consistent drilling centers across a large number of repeated trials. The research is bounded by the following parameters:

**1. Focus on Center Accuracy and Consistency.** The primary objective is to evaluate the tool's capacity to minimize radial and axial deviation from the intended drilling center. Effectiveness is quantified through statistical measures of positional accuracy (e.g., mean deviation, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation) across successive trials on identical workpieces.

**2. Alignment Guides' Functionality.** The study examines the mechanical design, engagement mechanism, and guiding behavior of the alignment guides. This includes assessing how the guides interact with the drill bit or pilot point, how they constrain lateral and angular displacement, and how they perform under varying insertion depths and feed conditions.

**3. Range of Workpiece Dimensions.** Performance is assessed across a defined spectrum of workpiece geometries, including variations in thickness, diameter (for cylindrical stock), and cross-sectional area (for flat stock). The dimensional boundaries are set by the tool's rated capacity and the practical limits of the test fixture.

**4. Material Variability.** The study incorporates a selection of representative materials spanning differing hardness, density, and machinability characteristics (e.g., mild steel, aluminum alloy, stainless steel, and a common polymer or wood composite). The intent is to observe how material response—chipping, deflection, and tool wear—interacts with the alignment guides.

**5. Establishing Capabilities and Limitations.** The research aims to delineate the operational envelope of the tool: the conditions under which it reliably maintains precision and the conditions under which its performance degrades. Findings are intended to provide practitioners and manufacturers with practical guidance on the tool's utility in common drilling scenarios.

**6. Repeated-Trial Design.** Consistency is evaluated through a controlled series of repeated trials (n ≥ 30 per test condition) to generate statistically meaningful data on repeatability and drift over time.

---

## Limitations

**1. Material and Dimensional Boundaries.** The study does not exhaustively cover every material or workpiece dimension. Findings are generalizable within the tested range but may not extrapolate reliably to extreme conditions (e.g., hardened tool steels above the tested hardness range, or workpieces beyond the tool's rated capacity).

**2. Controlled vs. Field Conditions.** Tests are conducted under controlled laboratory conditions—stable temperature, vibration isolation, and consistent lubrication. Real-world workshop environments introduce uncontrolled variables (thermal cycling, machine vibration, dust, inconsistent clamping) that may alter performance and are not fully replicated here.

**3. Operator Influence.** While operator technique is standardized through written protocols and training, residual variability in hand pressure, feed rate, and setup alignment remains a source of uncontrolled variation. The study cannot fully isolate the tool's contribution from operator-dependent factors.

**4. Machine and Tooling Constraints.** Results are specific to the particular drill press, spindle runout, and drill bit geometry used in the study. Differences in machine rigidity, spindle alignment, or bit condition in other setups may yield different outcomes. The study does not systematically vary the host machine.

**5. Single Tool Configuration.** The investigation focuses on one specific alignment guide design. It does not compare against alternative guiding mechanisms (e.g., self-centering bits, CNC-positioned drilling, or laser-guided systems), and therefore cannot rank this tool relative to other precision solutions.

**6. Static vs. Dynamic Loading.** The study primarily addresses quasi-static drilling operations. It does not extend to high-speed, high-feed, or interrupted-cut scenarios (e.g., drilling through seams, edges, or pre-existing holes) where dynamic forces may challenge the alignment guides differently.

**7. Wear and Longevity.** While repeated trials capture short-to-medium-term consistency, the study does not track performance degradation over extended tool life (hundreds or thousands of cycles). Long-term wear of the guide surfaces and their effect on precision remains outside the present scope.

**8. Measurement Resolution.** Accuracy is assessed using the measurement instruments available in the laboratory (e.g., digital calipers, dial indicators, or coordinate measuring devices). The resolution and calibration limits of these instruments impose a floor on the smallest detectable deviation, potentially masking sub-millimeter variations relevant to ultra-precision applications.

**9. Environmental Sensitivity.** Although temperature is controlled, the study does not quantify the effect of ambient humidity, thermal expansion of workpieces, or barometric changes on alignment performance.

**10. Economic and Ergonomic Factors.** The research addresses technical performance only. It does not evaluate the tool's cost-effectiveness, setup time, ergonomics, or learning curve for operators, all of which influence practical adoption.

---

*In summary, this study provides a focused, evidence-based assessment of the alignment guide tool's precision and repeatability within a defined set of materials, dimensions, and operating conditions. Its findings are most applicable to the scenarios tested and should be interpreted with awareness of the boundary conditions and uncontrolled variables outlined above.*

# Local Model-Serving Router — Architecture

## 1. Topology and process model

The single most important decision: **make the GPU-resident model a disposable child process, not a long-lived library loaded into the router.**

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  ROUTER (small, CPU-only, always up)        │
  interactive ─────►│  • admission control                        │
  client            │  • swap scheduler / priority queue          │
                    │  • session & KV cache index                 │
  benchmark   ─────►│  • memory ledger (predicted + measured)     │
  runner            │  • lease/heartbeat tracker                  │
                    │  • telemetry + reconciliation loop          │
                    └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                                    │ spawn / kill / signal
                    ┌───────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
                    │  WORKER (one at a time, GPU-resident)       │
                    │  • loads exactly one model                  │
                    │  • runs the inference loop                  │
                    │  • spills KV to CPU/disk on request         │
                    │  • checkpoints benchmark jobs               │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Why a child process instead of in-place load/unload:

- **Swap = kill + respawn.** When the child dies, the OS reclaims VRAM for you. In-place unload of a 70B model is where VRAM leaks live (half-released tensors, cached CUDA graphs, allocator arenas). A dead process can't leak.
- **Clean failure boundary.** A wedged model can't wedge the router. The router's job is to notice the child is dead and respawn.
- **The "one model at a time" constraint is about VRAM residency, not process count.** So you can keep *cold* workers alive — one per model, weights `mmap`'d from disk, not resident in VRAM. "Loading" model B then becomes a preload/page-in rather than a full process boot, cutting swap latency from ~minutes to ~seconds.

Recommendation: start with one hot worker (kill/respawn). Add cold workers per model as an optimization once swap latency is your bottleneck.

## 2. Scheduling core and swap policy

Three priority classes, and the asymmetry between them drives everything:

| Class | Meaning | Preemptible? | Resume cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0** | Interactive generation *in flight* | Never | — |
| **P1** | Interactive session idle, model still resident | Yes, after grace | High (KV loss → re-prompt) |
| **P2** | Benchmark job (queued or running) | Instantly | Low (checkpointed) |

The key insight: **benchmark jobs are cheap to preempt because they're checkpointed and resumable; interactive sessions are expensive because losing the KV cache means re-reading the whole transcript.** So the policy is asymmetric by construction:

- A benchmark job never evicts an *active* interactive session. It queues.
- A benchmark job evicts an *idle* interactive session only if `idle_time > T_grace` **and** the expected value of the queued work justifies the swap cost.
- An interactive request arriving while a benchmark runs **preempts the benchmark immediately** — spill its checkpoint, kill the worker, load the interactive model.

**Hysteresis against thrash.** Track measured swap cost (last few swaps) and require a cooldown before the next swap. A benchmark runner that fires 200 tiny jobs must not cause 200 model swaps — batch them against the *currently resident* model, and only swap when a different model has a backlog above a threshold. Concretely: swap when `Σ(benefit of queued jobs on model B) > k × measured_swap_cost`, with `k` tuned so a single job never triggers a swap.

The interactive model is effectively **pinned** for the daily-driver's working session and released only on idle timeout (`T_grace`, e.g. 60–120s). Benchmarks are scheduled *around* that pin, not in competition with it.

## 3. Session and KV caching

KV cache is the scarce interactive asset. Tier it by restore cost:

1. **VRAM** — while the model is resident. Fast, but competes with weights for the one budget.
2. **CPU RAM** — spill the *recent* prefix (last N turns) on eviction. Restore is a memcpy. **Bound this** — cap total spilled KV at a fraction of RAM so a dozen abandoned sessions can't OOM the host.
3. **Disk** — spill older prefixes. Slow restore, unbounded.
4. **Discard + re-prompt** — the fallback. On restore, re-run the full transcript as a prefill. This is usually *fine* for chat (the model re-reads the conversation) and costs one prefill, but continuations may diverge slightly from the original.

Practical rule: keep the last N turns in CPU RAM, spill the rest to disk, and on restore do a re-prompt from full history if the CPU-resident prefix was evicted. The router keeps a **session index** mapping `session_id → (model, KV location, last-active, lease)`.

For benchmarks there's no "session" to protect — they're stateless jobs with explicit checkpoints (which sample, which prompt, which tokens emitted so far), so a preempted benchmark resumes from its checkpoint, not from KV.

## 4. Request cancellation

Cancellation must be granular — "stop generating" is not "evict the model":

- **Interactive cancel (user hits escape):** abort the decode loop, **keep the prefix KV and keep the model resident.** The user will almost certainly continue the same conversation, so the prefix is reusable. Cancellation releases only the in-flight decode step.
- **Benchmark cancel:** kill the current batch, write the checkpoint, mark the job resumable, release the slot.

Mechanically: a cancellation token (a flag the inference loop checks between decode steps / between streamed chunks) propagated from the router into the worker. The worker must check it at every step boundary so a cancel lands within one token, not at the end of a 4k-token generation. On cancel, the worker returns a structured result (`aborted_at_step`, `kv_state`) so the router knows what to retain vs. release.

## 5. Memory accounting

VRAM is the one hard budget. The router must **predict before admitting**, not discover OOM after:

```
budget = VRAM_total − cuda_context − framework_overhead
resident = model_weights + kv_cache(max) + activation_scratch
```

The router estimates KV demand *per admitted request*:

```
kv_bytes ≈ seq_len × n_layers × n_kv_heads × head_dim × 2 × dtype_bytes   (Q+K, GQA-aware)
```

and uses it to (a) decide whether a request fits alongside the resident model, and (b) **cap `max_tokens` / batch size** so a runaway request can't OOM the box. Crucially, the ledger holds **two numbers per allocation — predicted and measured** — and the gap between them is itself a telemetry signal (see below). Reconcile the ledger against driver-level residency (`nvidia-smi` / CUDA stats) on a loop, because the ledger's belief and the GPU's reality diverge exactly when something is wrong.

## 6. Failure modes to instrument — ranked by blast radius

Order these by "how badly does it wedge the whole machine" and "how hard is it to detect":

1. **VRAM OOM mid-swap → zombie holding partial VRAM.** The #1 wedge. Worker dies partway through a load, leaves a process holding half the GPU, and the next load OOMs too. *Instrument:* worker exit codes, and a **reconciliation loop** comparing the router's "VRAM free" belief against driver-level residency. If they disagree, force-kill and re-measure before admitting anything.
2. **Zombie/orphan worker after crash.** Same family — VRAM accounting says free but it isn't. *Instrument:* lease/heartbeat per worker; a worker that misses its heartbeat gets SIGKILL'd and its VRAM reconciled.
3. **Hung decode (no tokens, no error).** Interactive user stares at a spinner forever. *Instrument:* a **token inter-arrival watchdog** — if no token for `T` seconds, kill the step and surface a real error instead of hanging.
4. **Thrash.** Swap rate too high, everything is slow. *Instrument:* swaps/min and swap-latency distribution as a first-class metric; alert when the scheduler is spending more time swapping than serving.
5. **Stale benchmark job holding a slot after its client disconnects.** *Instrument:* lease expiry — a job whose runner stopped heartbeating releases its slot.
6. **Silent KV corruption / quality degradation after spill-restore.** Hardest to detect; users just see worse answers. *Instrument:* restore latency and a sampled self-check (re-prompt a known prefix, compare a few tokens) to catch a corrupted spill.
7. **Thermal/power throttling throughput cliff.** *Instrument:* GPU clock + temperature telemetry correlated with token/s, so a cliff is attributed to thermals not a bug.
8. **Disk full on KV spill or weight cache.** *Instrument:* free-space guard that refuses to spill (and degrades to re-prompt) before the spill itself fails mid-write.

## Build order

1. Router + kill/respawn worker + lease/heartbeat + VRAM reconciliation loop. (This buys you the #1 and #2 failure modes, which are the ones that brick the machine.)
2. Memory ledger with predict-before-admit and `max_tokens` capping.
3. Swap scheduler with the P0/P1/P2 asymmetry, hysteresis, and benchmark checkpointing.
4. Tiered KV spill + session index.
5. Cold workers per model to cut swap latency, only if profiling shows swap time is the bottleneck.

The through-line: the router is a small, boring, always-alive CPU process whose entire job is to *believe the GPU's actual state* and to treat every GPU-resident model as something it can afford to kill. Everything else — caching, swapping, cancellation — is policy layered on that.

# Local Model-Serving Router — Architecture

## Topology

```
                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │              ROUTER (single process)         │
                        │                                             │
  Interactive client ──►│  Admission    Scheduler    Swap Engine      │
  (HTTP/SSE, 1 conn)    │  Control ──►  (priority  ──►  (load/unload)│
                        │  (auth,      queue)         ──►  Model      │
  Benchmark runner ────►│   rate-limit,    │              Registry    │
  (gRPC batch, N jobs)  │   session TTL)   │              (1 slot)    │
                        │                 ▼                          │
                        │           Memory Ledger ◄── CUDA            │
                        │           (VRAM budget)      driver        │
                        │                 │                          │
                        └─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘
                                          ▼
                                    ┌──────────────┐
                                    │  GPU (1 slot)│
                                    │  model + KV  │
                                    └──────────────┘
```

One router process, one GPU, one model resident at a time. The router is the only thing that touches the model lifecycle. Clients never talk to the inference backend directly.

---

## 1. Admission Control

Two queues, one priority rule:

| Class | Queue | Admission rule |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive | `iq` (FIFO, max depth 1) | Always admitted. If the requested model ≠ resident model, the request enters a **swap-wait** state and the client receives a `202` with an ETA header, not a silent hang. |
| Benchmark | `bq` (FIFO, max depth 32) | Admitted only when the resident model matches *and* no interactive request is pending. Otherwise it parks. |

The interactive queue is depth-1 by design. A human generates one turn at a time; anything deeper is a bug or a script masquerading as a user. Reject the second concurrent interactive request with `429` and a reason.

Benchmark jobs declare their model, batch size, and expected duration at submission. The router uses that metadata for swap scheduling (below).

---

## 2. Model Registry and the Single Slot

The registry is a small in-memory table (persisted to a JSON file so restarts don't lose warm-model hints):

```
{
  "slot": {
    "model_id": "llama-3-70b-instruct",
    "loaded_at": 1717000000,
    "last_used_at": 1717000042,
    "kv_cache_bytes": 838860800,
    "weights_bytes": 140000000000
  },
  "candidates": {
    "llama-3-70b-instruct": { "load_time_s": 52, "weights_bytes": 140e9 },
    "mistral-7b":          { "load_time_s": 4,  "weights_bytes": 13e9 }
  }
}
```

`load_time_s` is measured on first load and updated on every subsequent load (cold page cache vs warm). The swap engine uses it to compute ETAs.

The slot is guarded by a single mutex. Only the swap engine acquires it. Generation requests acquire a lighter "model-in-use" lease so the swap engine can't yank the model out from under a running decode step.

---

## 3. Swap Policy

This is the part that makes or breaks the system. The policy is a **cost-aware preempt-or-wait** decision, evaluated when an interactive request arrives and the resident model doesn't match.

```
on interactive_request(model M):
    if resident == M:
        serve immediately
        return

    resident = current model
    bench_remaining = bq.front().expected_remaining_s   # 0 if bq empty

    swap_cost = registry[M].load_time_s + bench_loss(bench)

    if bench_remaining < SWAP_THRESHOLD (≈ 90 s):
        # benchmark is close to done; let it finish, then swap
        park request, ETA = bench_remaining + swap_cost
    elif bench_remaining > BENCH_GRACE (≈ 300 s) and bench_progress > 0.8:
        # benchmark is 80%+ done; finish it
        park request, ETA = bench_remaining + swap_cost
    else:
        # preempt now
        cancel bench batch (checkpoint if supported)
        swap to M
        serve
```

Key parameters and why:

- **Sticky dwell**: after serving an interactive turn, the model stays resident for `STICKY_S = 120 s`. Follow-up turns (which are the common case) hit a warm model. The benchmark queue is blocked during this window.
- **Swap cooldown**: minimum `COOLDOWN_S = 60 s` between any two swaps. Prevents thrash when a user switches models rapidly.
- **Benchmark checkpointing**: if the benchmark framework supports it (e.g., it can save completed samples to disk), the swap engine signals a graceful stop at the next sample boundary rather than killing mid-generation. If it doesn't, the swap engine kills the process and the benchmark runner re-submits from its last checkpoint.

The policy is deliberately simple. A learned scheduler is the wrong tool for one machine with two traffic classes; a decision tree with three branches is debuggable.

---

## 4. Session Caching

Two layers, because "session cache" means different things at different timescales:

**KV cache (in-VRAM, per active sequence).**
The inference backend (llama.cpp, vLLM, whatever) manages this. The router's only concern is the memory ledger (below). When the user stops a generation, the router tells the backend to release the KV block for that sequence immediately, not at turn end. This reclaims VRAM for the next turn or a swap.

**Model residency TTL (the real "session cache").**
With one model slot, the only way to keep a session fast is to keep its model loaded. The router tracks `last_used_at` per model. The swap engine treats a model with `last_used_at` within `STICKY_S` as "hot" and resists evicting it for a benchmark job. A benchmark job that wants a *different* model must wait for the sticky window to expire or the interactive user to go idle for `IDLE_EVICT_S = 300 s`.

**CPU-side prompt cache (optional, cheap).**
If the interactive client sends long system prompts repeatedly, cache the tokenized prompt bytes in RAM. Re-tokenization is fast enough that this is a minor optimization, but it avoids a 200 ms hiccup on model swap.

---

## 5. Request Cancellation

Three cancellation sources, each with different semantics:

| Source | Scope | Action |
|---|---|---|
| User hits Stop | One generation | Backend aborts decode loop, releases KV block. Router marks sequence done. Model stays resident. |
| User closes tab / disconnects | One session | Same as above, plus start the `IDLE_EVICT_S` countdown. |
| Swap engine preempts benchmark | Entire benchmark batch | Signal SIGTERM to benchmark process. Wait `GRACE_S = 10 s`. SIGKILL if still alive. Acquire slot mutex. Unload. Load new model. |

The critical invariant: **cancellation must be synchronous with respect to the slot mutex.** The swap engine must not begin unloading until the backend confirms all in-flight sequences are drained and KV is freed. Otherwise you get a CUDA context that's half-torn-down and the next load fails with a cryptic driver error.

Implementation: the backend exposes a `drain(timeout)` call. The swap engine calls it, blocks, and only proceeds on success or timeout. On timeout, it escalates to a full backend process restart (kill + relaunch), which is the nuclear option but the only reliable way to recover a wedged CUDA context.

---

## 6. Memory Accounting

A **Memory Ledger** object in the router tracks VRAM in bytes, not percentages. The budget is `TOTAL_VRAM` (queried once at startup via `nvidia-smi` / `cudaDeviceGetProperties`).

```
TOTAL_VRAM
  ├── cuda_context        (~800 MB, fixed, measured once)
  ├── model_weights       (from registry, known before load)
  ├── kv_cache_allocated  (backend reports after each batch)
  ├── activations_peak    (backend reports, high-water mark per sequence)
  └── free               (computed; must stay > MIN_FREE)
```

Rules:

- **Pre-load check**: before loading model M, the ledger verifies `free ≥ weights(M) + MIN_KV + MIN_FREE`. `MIN_KV` is the KV for one interactive sequence at the model's max context (e.g., 4096 tokens × 2 × 8 bytes × n_layers). `MIN_FREE` is a 2 GB safety margin for CUDA allocations and fragmentation. If the check fails, the swap is refused and the request is rejected with a clear error.

- **Post-load verification**: after the backend reports the model is loaded, the ledger reads actual VRAM usage. If it exceeds the predicted budget by more than 10%, log a warning (the model's real memory footprint differs from the config estimate — this happens with some quantization formats).

- **KV growth guard**: the backend reports `kv_cache_allocated` after every generation step. If it approaches `free - MIN_FREE`, the router truncates the context (drops oldest KV blocks) rather than letting the backend OOM. This is the interactive equivalent of a context-window limit, enforced by the router rather than the backend.

- **Fragmentation tracking**: log `free` after every swap. If `free` after unload is less than `free` before load (i.e., the GPU didn't give memory back), increment a fragmentation counter. After 3 consecutive swaps with growing fragmentation, trigger a backend restart to reclaim.

---

## 7. Failure Modes to Instrument First

Ordered by "how much pain this causes and how hard it is to debug without telemetry":

### 7.1 OOM during model load
**What happens**: The backend starts loading a 140 GB model into 80 GB of VRAM. It allocates 40 GB, hits the wall, and either crashes or (worse) leaves a half-loaded model that holds VRAM but can't serve.
**Instrument**: The pre-load check in §6 catches the obvious case. For the subtle case (model loads but KV allocation fails on first request), instrument the backend's first-token latency and VRAM delta. If `free < 0` after load, treat as a failed load: unload, log, reject.
**Alert**: any OOM event. This is a config error or a model that's too big for the hardware.

### 7.2 Swap thrash
**What happens**: User switches between two models every 40 seconds. The swap engine loads/unloads in a loop. The machine is 100% busy loading models and serves nothing.
**Instrument**: Count swaps in a sliding 10-minute window. If `swaps > 5`, the cooldown should have prevented this. If it didn't, the cooldown timer is broken or the user is hammering the API. Log the model sequence. Alert at `swaps > 8`.
**Mitigation**: The cooldown in §3 is the primary defense. The alert is the backstop.

### 7.3 Interactive latency regression
**What happens**: A benchmark job that's "supposed to be background" is actually consuming all the compute, and interactive requests get 12-second time-to-first-token instead of 1.5 seconds.
**Instrument**: Track `time_to_first_token` and `tokens_per_second` per request, tagged with the traffic class. Alert if interactive p99 TTFT > 5 s over a 5-minute window. This is the single most important metric for the daily-driver experience.
**Mitigation**: The admission control in §1 blocks benchmark admission when interactive traffic is active. If TTFT still degrades, the benchmark is running *on the same model* as the interactive user and stealing compute. The router should throttle benchmark batch size to leave headroom (e.g., cap benchmark concurrent sequences at 1 when an interactive session is active).

### 7.4 Zombie GPU memory after crash
**What happens**: The backend process segfaults. The OS reclaims the process but the CUDA context (and its VRAM) is not released until the GPU driver reclaims it, which can take 30+ seconds or never happen if the driver is wedged.
**Instrument**: After any backend process exit (expected or not), poll `nvidia-smi` for 30 seconds. If the GPU's memory usage doesn't drop to the baseline (~800 MB context), escalate: kill any orphaned child processes, then `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` (if available), then alert a human.
**This is the failure mode that turns a 5-second hiccup into a "I have to reboot the machine" event.**

### 7.5 Benchmark starvation
**What happens**: The interactive user is active 16 hours a day. The benchmark job has been parked for 22 hours. It never runs.
**Instrument**: Track `bq.front().age`. Alert at 1 hour. The swap policy in §3 should eventually let it run during the sticky window, but if the user is genuinely active 24/7, the benchmark will never get a slot. This is a policy problem, not a code bug — the alert tells the user their benchmark is stuck.
**Mitigation**: The benchmark runner should declare a `deadline`. If it misses the deadline, the router cancels it and reports the reason.

### 7.6 Stale session after model swap
**What happens**: User has a 50-turn conversation with model A. The model gets evicted for a benchmark. User sends turn 51. The router loads model A, but the KV cache is gone, so the model has no memory of turns 1–50. It responds as if the conversation just started.
**Instrument**: Track `session_turn_count` and `kv_cache_present`. If a request arrives with `turn_count > 1` and `kv_cache_present == false`, log a `session_amnesia` event. This is expected behavior, but the client should be told: the router returns a `session_reset: true` flag so the client can re-inject the conversation history.
**Mitigation**: The sticky dwell in §4 minimizes this. For long sessions, the client-side prompt cache (§4) re-injects history.

---

## 8. Process Model

The router is a single long-running process (Rust or Go; the scheduler and ledger need to be fast and the memory model simple). The inference backend is a **child process** that the router spawns and can kill. This is the single most important architectural decision:

- The backend owns the CUDA context. Killing the process is the only reliable way to reclaim a wedged context.
- The router communicates with the backend over a local Unix socket with a simple JSON-RPC protocol: `load(model)`, `unload()`, `generate(prompt, max_tokens, stream)`, `drain(timeout)`, `report_memory()`.
- The backend is stateless across restarts. All session state lives in the router.

If the backend dies, the router detects it (socket EOF or heartbeat timeout at 5 s), marks the slot empty, and the next request triggers a fresh spawn + load. The user sees a gap, not a crash.

---

## 9. What I Would Not Do

- **No GPU sharing / MPS / MIG.** With one model slot, there's nothing to share. MPS adds a failure mode (one process's OOM kills the other) for zero benefit.
- **No model quantization switching at runtime.** If the user wants a smaller model, they request it by name and the router swaps. The router doesn't decide to quantize the loaded model to fit.
- **No learned scheduler.** Three traffic classes on one machine doesn't need reinforcement learning. A decision tree with logged decisions is debuggable in an afternoon. A learned policy is a black box you debug by turning it off.
- **No multi-GPU.** The constraint is one machine, one model. If you have two GPUs, that's a different architecture (two slots, round-robin). Don't solve that problem here.

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Problem Framing

"Triage" in radiology means **prioritizing and routing studies**, not diagnosis. Concretely, the system answers:

- **Urgency scoring**: Is this a 10-minute emergency (massive PE, pneumothorax, fracture) or a 2-day routine read?
- **Routing**: Send to the right subspecialty (neuroradiology, musculoskeletal, cardiothoracic).
- **Findings flagging**: Surface candidate findings (nodule, effusion, fracture) as bounding boxes or whole-image attention maps so the radiologist reviews the right region first.

This is a **multi-task classification + detection** problem, not a single binary classifier.

---

## 2. Model Architecture

### 2A. Backbone: Vision Transformer (ViT) or ConvNeXt

For 2D CT/MR slices, a **ViT-L/16** or **ConvNeXt-XL** backbone is the current strong default.

```
Input: 224×224 or 384×384 pixel patch (DICOM slice, resampled to 1mm isotropic if 3D)
  → Patch embedding (16×16 patches)
  → 24 transformer layers, 1024-dim, 16 heads
  → [CLS] token → Urgency head (7-class ordinal regression)
  → Per-patch tokens → Detection head (DETR-style, 92 COCO-style classes)
```

**Why ViT over ResNet-50 here:**
- Handles multi-scale pathology (a 3mm pulmonary nodule and a 12cm mass in the same volume) better with global attention.
- Pretrained weights (MAE, DINOv2) transfer well to medical imaging when fine-tuned with a **linear probing → full fine-tune** schedule.

If your data is 3D (CT volumes), use a **3D ViT** (e.g., Swin-3D or a 3D ConvNeXt) operating on 128³ patches, or a **2D-slice ensemble** (read every Nth slice, aggregate with a small GRU/attention pooler) if GPU memory is constrained.

### 2B. Multi-Task Heads

```python
class TriageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, backbone, num_urgency=7, num_findings=92):
        self.backbone = backbone          # ViT-L/16, returns [CLS] + patch tokens
        self.urgency_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(512, 7)             # ordinal: routine → stat
        )
        self.finding_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(512, num_findings)  # multi-label sigmoid
        )
        self.det_head = DETRDecoder(      # optional: bounding boxes
            num_queries=100, num_classes=num_findings
        )
```

**Urgency as ordinal regression**, not 7 independent classes. Use **CORAL loss** (Cao et al. 2020) so misclassifying "routine" as "urgent" costs less than "massive PE" as "routine."

### 2C. Modality Handling

- **X-ray / CT / MRI / US** share the backbone but have **modality-specific adapter layers** (LoRA-style low-rank adapters on the transformer attention, ~1% of params) so you don't retrain everything per modality.
- DICOM pixel data must go through a **modality-aware normalization**: window/level per modality (lung, mediastinum, bone, brain windows for CT; no windowing for X-ray; N4 bias correction + z-score for MRI).

---

## 3. Training Pipeline

### 3A. Data

- **Source**: Anonymized DICOM studies from your own PACS (with IRB/ethics approval) + public datasets (NIH ChestXray14, RSNA, CT-RATE, MedNIST) for pretraining.
- **Labels**: Urgency scores from radiologist reports (NER-extract "STAT," "urgent," "routine" from structured HL7 ORU reports). Finding labels from structured report fields or manual annotation.
- **Scale**: Aim for ≥50k studies for the backbone, ≥10k per urgency class. Class imbalance is severe (95%+ are routine) → use **focal loss** and **class-balanced sampling**.

### 3B. Training Loop

```
Phase 1 (pretrain, 2-4 weeks on 8×A100):
  MAE / DINOv2 self-supervised on 1M unlabeled DICOM slices
  → modality-specific adapters

Phase 2 (supervised fine-tune, 1-2 weeks):
  Full backbone + heads, AdamW, lr=1e-4 → 1e-6 cosine schedule
  3D augmentation: random rotation ±15°, elastic deform, intensity jitter
  2D augmentation: flip, rotation, CutMix
  Loss: CORAL(urgency) + 0.5 * BCEWithLogits(findings) + 1.0 * DETR loss

Phase 3 (calibration):
  Temperature scaling on a held-out validation set
  → calibrated probability outputs (critical for clinical trust)
```

### 3C. Validation

- **Patient-level split** (not study-level) to avoid leakage.
- Report **sensitivity at fixed specificity** (e.g., "catch 95% of STATs at 90% specificity") rather than AUC alone. Radiologists care about missed emergencies, not aggregate discrimination.
- Slice by modality, body part, and urgency class.

---

## 4. PACS Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific.

### 4A. DICOM Network Architecture

```
┌──────────────┐    DICOM C-MOVE/C-STORE     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Modalities  │ ──────────────────────────► │     PACS        │
│ (CT, MR, US) │   (DICOM 3.0, port 104)    │ (Orthanc /      │
└──────────────┘                             │  dcm4chee /     │
                                              │  AWS HealthImaging)
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          DICOMweb (QIDO-RS, WADO-RS)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  Triage Service │
                                              │  (FastAPI +    │
                                              │   PyTorch)     │
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          HL7 FHIR (Observation,
                                          DiagnosticReport)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  RIS / Worklist │
                                              │  (prioritized)  │
                                              └────────────────┘
```

### 4B. PACS Choice

| PACS | Why |
|---|---|
| **Orthanc** (self-hosted) | Lightweight, DICOMweb native, Python plugin API, great for dev/test. Not for production volume. |
| **dcm4chee** (self-hosted) | DICOM 3.0 fully compliant, handles C-STORE/C-FIND at scale, DICOMweb built-in. Best open-source production choice. |
| **AWS HealthImaging Archive** | Managed, DICOMweb + FHIR native, scales to millions of studies. Avoids running your own PACS ops. |
| **Existing hospital PACS** (GE, Philips, Agfa) | Integrate via DICOM C-MOVE or DICOMweb if the vendor supports it. Check DICOM conformance statements. |

### 4C. The Triage Service (DICOMweb → Model → FHIR)

```python
# FastAPI service, deployed as a container
@app.post("/triage/{study_uid}")
async def triage_study(study_uid: str):
    # 1. Retrieve DICOM objects via DICOMweb WADO-RS
    #    GET /studies/{study_uid}/series/{series_uid}/instances
    #    → retrieve DICOM bytes, parse with pydicom
    dicom_objects = fetch_dicomweb(pacs_url, study_uid)

    # 2. Preprocess: resample to 1mm iso, apply modality windowing
    tensors = preprocess(dicom_objects)  # → list of 2D or 3D tensors

    # 3. Inference (batch all slices, or 3D volume)
    urgency, findings, boxes = model(tensors)

    # 4. Write back as FHIR resources
    fhir_observations = to_fhir(urgency, findings, boxes)
    post_fhir_bundle(ris_fhir_url, fhir_observations)

    # 5. Update the study's priority in the RIS worklist
    #    (HL7 ORU^R01 or FHIR DiagnosticReport.status)
    update_worklist_priority(study_uid, urgency_class)

    return {"urgency": urgency, "findings": findings}
```

### 4D. Triggering the Pipeline

- **DICOM C-STORE notification**: PACS fires a callback (HL7 ADT/ORM or DICOM DIMSE C-STORE event) when a study arrives. The triage service subscribes and pulls the study via DICOMweb.
- **Polling fallback**: If the PACS doesn't support push notifications, poll QIDO-RS every 10-30s for new studies. Ugly but works.

### 4E. GPU Sizing

- ViT-L/16 on 2D slices: ~4GB VRAM per study. An **A10 (24GB)** or **T4 (16GB)** handles ~3-4 studies in parallel.
- 3D CT volumes: ~12-16GB. Use an **A100 40GB** or **L40S**.
- For a single-center deployment (500-2000 studies/day), **one A100** with a queue (Redis + Celery or a simple asyncio queue) is sufficient. Latency target: **< 30s per study** for triage scoring.

### 4F. Serving the Model

- **TorchServe** or **Triton Inference Server** for the PyTorch model.
- Put a **DICOM preprocessing worker** (pydicom + numpy) in front — it's CPU-bound and shouldn't block GPU inference.
- Run the whole thing in **Kubernetes** (or a single Docker Compose stack for one site):
  - `triage-api` (FastAPI, 2 replicas)
  - `triage-worker` (GPU pod, 1-2 replicas)
  - `redis` (job queue)
  - `orthanc` or connect to existing PACS

---

## 5. Regulatory & Clinical Integration

- **FDA / CE marking**: In the US, this is a **Class II SaMD** (510(k) pathway). You need a predicate device, a well-defined intended use ("prioritization of studies"), and a clinical validation study. The AI doesn't diagnose — it prioritizes — which is a more tractable regulatory path.
- **HIPAA / GDPR**: DICOM de-identification (remove PHI tags per DICOM PS3.15), BAA with cloud PACS provider, audit logging of every inference.
- **Integration with the radiologist's workflow**: The output should appear as **overlays in the existing PACS viewer** (e.g., OHIF, which supports DICOMweb and can render FHIR annotations) or as a **worklist reorder** in the RIS. Don't build a separate viewer.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: The AI scores urgency; a radiologist confirms. Log every disagreement for model monitoring and retraining.

---

## 6. Monitoring & Iteration

- Track **urgency calibration drift** weekly (reliability diagrams on the last 500 studies).
- Alert if sensitivity for STAT-class drops below threshold.
- Collect radiologist corrections (click to accept/reject a finding flag) → feed into a **semi-supervised or active-learning** retraining loop quarterly.

---

**TL;DR stack**: ViT-L/16 backbone with modality adapters + CORAL urgency head + DETR finding boxes, trained in 3 phases (SSL → fine-tune → calibrate), served via TorchServe behind a FastAPI DICOMweb client, pulling from dcm4chee or AWS HealthImaging, writing FHIR Observations back to the RIS worklist, deployed on one A100 in Kubernetes.

Want me to go deeper on any piece — the DICOM conformance details, the CORAL loss implementation, the FHIR resource mapping, or the clinical validation study design?

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Problem Framing

"Triage" in radiology means **prioritizing and routing studies**, not diagnosis. Concretely, the system answers:

- **Urgency scoring**: Is this a 10-minute emergency (massive PE, pneumothorax, fracture) or a 2-day routine read?
- **Routing**: Send to the right subspecialty (neuroradiology, musculoskeletal, cardiothoracic).
- **Findings flagging**: Surface candidate findings (nodule, effusion, fracture) as bounding boxes or whole-image attention maps so the radiologist reviews the right region first.

This is a **multi-task classification + detection** problem, not a single binary classifier.

---

## 2. Model Architecture

### 2A. Backbone: Vision Transformer (ViT) or ConvNeXt

For 2D CT/MR slices, a **ViT-L/16** or **ConvNeXt-XL** backbone is the current strong default.

```
Input: 224×224 or 384×384 pixel patch (DICOM slice, resampled to 1mm isotropic if 3D)
  → Patch embedding (16×16 patches)
  → 24 transformer layers, 1024-dim, 16 heads
  → [CLS] token → Urgency head (7-class ordinal regression)
  → Per-patch tokens → Detection head (DETR-style, 92 COCO-style classes)
```

**Why ViT over ResNet-50 here:**
- Handles multi-scale pathology (a 3mm pulmonary nodule and a 12cm mass in the same volume) better with global attention.
- Pretrained weights (MAE, DINOv2) transfer well to medical imaging when fine-tuned with a **linear probing → full fine-tune** schedule.

If your data is 3D (CT volumes), use a **3D ViT** (e.g., Swin-3D or a 3D ConvNeXt) operating on 128³ patches, or a **2D-slice ensemble** (read every Nth slice, aggregate with a small GRU/attention pooler) if GPU memory is constrained.

### 2B. Multi-Task Heads

```python
class TriageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, backbone, num_urgency=7, num_findings=92):
        self.backbone = backbone          # ViT-L/16, returns [CLS] + patch tokens
        self.urgency_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(512, 7)             # ordinal: routine → stat
        )
        self.finding_head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(512, num_findings)  # multi-label sigmoid
        )
        self.det_head = DETRDecoder(      # optional: bounding boxes
            num_queries=100, num_classes=num_findings
        )
```

**Urgency as ordinal regression**, not 7 independent classes. Use **CORAL loss** (Cao et al. 2020) so misclassifying "routine" as "urgent" costs less than "massive PE" as "routine."

### 2C. Modality Handling

- **X-ray / CT / MRI / US** share the backbone but have **modality-specific adapter layers** (LoRA-style low-rank adapters on the transformer attention, ~1% of params) so you don't retrain everything per modality.
- DICOM pixel data must go through a **modality-aware normalization**: window/level per modality (lung, mediastinum, bone, brain windows for CT; no windowing for X-ray; N4 bias correction + z-score for MRI).

---

## 3. Training Pipeline

### 3A. Data

- **Source**: Anonymized DICOM studies from your own PACS (with IRB/ethics approval) + public datasets (NIH ChestXray14, RSNA, CT-RATE, MedNIST) for pretraining.
- **Labels**: Urgency scores from radiologist reports (NER-extract "STAT," "urgent," "routine" from structured HL7 ORU reports). Finding labels from structured report fields or manual annotation.
- **Scale**: Aim for ≥50k studies for the backbone, ≥10k per urgency class. Class imbalance is severe (95%+ are routine) → use **focal loss** and **class-balanced sampling**.

### 3B. Training Loop

```
Phase 1 (pretrain, 2-4 weeks on 8×A100):
  MAE / DINOv2 self-supervised on 1M unlabeled DICOM slices
  → modality-specific adapters

Phase 2 (supervised fine-tune, 1-2 weeks):
  Full backbone + heads, AdamW, lr=1e-4 → 1e-6 cosine schedule
  3D augmentation: random rotation ±15°, elastic deform, intensity jitter
  2D augmentation: flip, rotation, CutMix
  Loss: CORAL(urgency) + 0.5 * BCEWithLogits(findings) + 1.0 * DETR loss

Phase 3 (calibration):
  Temperature scaling on a held-out validation set
  → calibrated probability outputs (critical for clinical trust)
```

### 3C. Validation

- **Patient-level split** (not study-level) to avoid leakage.
- Report **sensitivity at fixed specificity** (e.g., "catch 95% of STATs at 90% specificity") rather than AUC alone. Radiologists care about missed emergencies, not aggregate discrimination.
- Slice by modality, body part, and urgency class.

---

## 4. PACS Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific.

### 4A. DICOM Network Architecture

```
┌──────────────┐    DICOM C-MOVE/C-STORE     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Modalities  │ ──────────────────────────► │     PACS        │
│ (CT, MR, US) │   (DICOM 3.0, port 104)    │ (Orthanc /      │
└──────────────┘                             │  dcm4chee /     │
                                              │  AWS HealthImaging)
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          DICOMweb (QIDO-RS, WADO-RS)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  Triage Service │
                                              │  (FastAPI +    │
                                              │   PyTorch)     │
                                              └───────┬────────┘
                                                      │
                                          HL7 FHIR (Observation,
                                          DiagnosticReport)
                                                      │
                                              ┌───────▼────────┐
                                              │  RIS / Worklist │
                                              │  (prioritized)  │
                                              └────────────────┘
```

### 4B. PACS Choice

| PACS | Why |
|---|---|
| **Orthanc** (self-hosted) | Lightweight, DICOMweb native, Python plugin API, great for dev/test. Not for production volume. |
| **dcm4chee** (self-hosted) | DICOM 3.0 fully compliant, handles C-STORE/C-FIND at scale, DICOMweb built-in. Best open-source production choice. |
| **AWS HealthImaging Archive** | Managed, DICOMweb + FHIR native, scales to millions of studies. Avoids running your own PACS ops. |
| **Existing hospital PACS** (GE, Philips, Agfa) | Integrate via DICOM C-MOVE or DICOMweb if the vendor supports it. Check DICOM conformance statements. |

### 4C. The Triage Service (DICOMweb → Model → FHIR)

```python
# FastAPI service, deployed as a container
@app.post("/triage/{study_uid}")
async def triage_study(study_uid: str):
    # 1. Retrieve DICOM objects via DICOMweb WADO-RS
    #    GET /studies/{study_uid}/series/{series_uid}/instances
    #    → retrieve DICOM bytes, parse with pydicom
    dicom_objects = fetch_dicomweb(pacs_url, study_uid)

    # 2. Preprocess: resample to 1mm iso, apply modality windowing
    tensors = preprocess(dicom_objects)  # → list of 2D or 3D tensors

    # 3. Inference (batch all slices, or 3D volume)
    urgency, findings, boxes = model(tensors)

    # 4. Write back as FHIR resources
    fhir_observations = to_fhir(urgency, findings, boxes)
    post_fhir_bundle(ris_fhir_url, fhir_observations)

    # 5. Update the study's priority in the RIS worklist
    #    (HL7 ORU^R01 or FHIR DiagnosticReport.status)
    update_worklist_priority(study_uid, urgency_class)

    return {"urgency": urgency, "findings": findings}
```

### 4D. Triggering the Pipeline

- **DICOM C-STORE notification**: PACS fires a callback (HL7 ADT/ORM or DICOM DIMSE C-STORE event) when a study arrives. The triage service subscribes and pulls the study via DICOMweb.
- **Polling fallback**: If the PACS doesn't support push notifications, poll QIDO-RS every 10-30s for new studies. Ugly but works.

### 4E. GPU Sizing

- ViT-L/16 on 2D slices: ~4GB VRAM per study. An **A10 (24GB)** or **T4 (16GB)** handles ~3-4 studies in parallel.
- 3D CT volumes: ~12-16GB. Use an **A100 40GB** or **L40S**.
- For a single-center deployment (500-2000 studies/day), **one A100** with a queue (Redis + Celery or a simple asyncio queue) is sufficient. Latency target: **< 30s per study** for triage scoring.

### 4F. Serving the Model

- **TorchServe** or **Triton Inference Server** for the PyTorch model.
- Put a **DICOM preprocessing worker** (pydicom + numpy) in front — it's CPU-bound and shouldn't block GPU inference.
- Run the whole thing in **Kubernetes** (or a single Docker Compose stack for one site):
  - `triage-api` (FastAPI, 2 replicas)
  - `triage-worker` (GPU pod, 1-2 replicas)
  - `redis` (job queue)
  - `orthanc` or connect to existing PACS

---

## 5. Regulatory & Clinical Integration

- **FDA / CE marking**: In the US, this is a **Class II SaMD** (510(k) pathway). You need a predicate device, a well-defined intended use ("prioritization of studies"), and a clinical validation study. The AI doesn't diagnose — it prioritizes — which is a more tractable regulatory path.
- **HIPAA / GDPR**: DICOM de-identification (remove PHI tags per DICOM PS3.15), BAA with cloud PACS provider, audit logging of every inference.
- **Integration with the radiologist's workflow**: The output should appear as **overlays in the existing PACS viewer** (e.g., OHIF, which supports DICOMweb and can render FHIR annotations) or as a **worklist reorder** in the RIS. Don't build a separate viewer.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: The AI scores urgency; a radiologist confirms. Log every disagreement for model monitoring and retraining.

---

## 6. Monitoring & Iteration

- Track **urgency calibration drift** weekly (reliability diagrams on the last 500 studies).
- Alert if sensitivity for STAT-class drops below threshold.
- Collect radiologist corrections (click to accept/reject a finding flag) → feed into a **semi-supervised or active-learning** retraining loop quarterly.

---

**TL;DR stack**: ViT-L/16 backbone with modality adapters + CORAL urgency head + DETR finding boxes, trained in 3 phases (SSL → fine-tune → calibrate), served via TorchServe behind a FastAPI DICOMweb client, pulling from dcm4chee or AWS HealthImaging, writing FHIR Observations back to the RIS worklist, deployed on one A100 in Kubernetes.

Taming Verbatim Repetition Loops in Long-Chain-of-Thought Models Why the Loops Happen (one-paragraph root-cause) Once a thinking model emits a short pattern of tokens, the autoregressive conditional P(next | last N) becomes dominated by that pattern: attention collapses onto the most recent window, the KV cache is "saturated" with the same content, and the next token is near-certainly the one that continues the loop. The loop is self-reinforcing at every level—sampling, attention, and context—so a single intervention is rarely enough. The interventions below attack different links in that chain. --- 1 · SAMPLING (how the next token is drawn from the distribution)

| # | Technique | How it helps | Quality risk |
|---|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| S1 | **Adaptive n-gram block** – if the last *k* tokens (k = 4–8) match a span that appeared ≥ 2× earlier in the same generation, resample from a truncated distribution that excludes the matching continuation. | Directly severs the self-reinforcing conditional. | Low if k is small; can suppress legitimate re-use of a phrase. Tune k per domain. |
| S2 | **Frequency / presence penalty with a decay window** – apply a penalty only to tokens in the last *W* positions (W ≈ 512–2048), not the whole history. | Breaks the local loop without globally flattening the distribution. | Moderate; too-wide a window hurts coherence. |
| S3 | **Two-temperature schedule** – use T ≈ 0.3 for "reasoning" spans, bump to T ≈ 0.8–1.0 for "transition" spans (detected by a lightweight classifier or by entropy spikes). | Lets the model escape a low-entropy attractor without injecting noise into the reasoning itself. | Requires a transition detector; misclassification adds noise. |
| S4 | **Top-p with a floor** – keep p ≥ 0.95 so the distribution never collapses to a single token, even in high-confidence loop states. | Prevents the "one-token attractor" that makes loops deterministic. | Minimal; the floor is wide enough to preserve quality. |
| S5 | **Stochastic beam with a diversity penalty** – keep *B* = 3–5 beams; penalise beams whose last 16 tokens overlap heavily with another beam. | Provides multiple "escape routes" out of a loop state. | Higher compute per token; beam search is ~3–5× slower. |

--- 2 · DECODING / ARCHITECTURE (how the model computes logits)

| # | Technique | How it helps | Quality risk |
|---|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| D1 | **Sliding-window + summary KV cache** – keep full KV for the first 1 k tokens, a compressed "summary" block for the middle, and a full window for the most recent 1 k. Periodically re-summarise. | Prevents attention from being dominated by a stale repetitive window; forces the model to "re-orient." | Summary may lose a needed detail; needs a good summariser. |
| D2 | **Attention-entropy monitor + head re-routing** – if the entropy of the attention distribution over the last 256 keys drops below a threshold (attention "collapses"), reduce the weight of the most-attended keys or inject a small random perturbation into the Q/K of the next layer. | Attacks the recency-bias mechanism at the source. | Perturbation magnitude is a hyperparameter; too large → incoherence. |
| D3 | **Position-encoding jitter / relative-bias re-anchoring** – every *M* tokens, shift the relative position bias so the model no longer treats "the last 64 tokens" as a privileged window. | Breaks the positional prior that makes "continue the last pattern" the default. | Requires model surgery; may hurt long-range coherence if overdone. |
| D4 | **Auxiliary "progress" head** – a small classifier head (trained jointly) that predicts "is the model making new information?" at each step. When it fires "stuck," gate the main logits through a diversity filter. | Gives the model an internal signal it's looping, without external heuristics. | Needs a training pass; the head must be well-calibrated. |
| D5 | **KV-cache pruning of low-diversity spans** – if a contiguous KV block has near-identical value vectors, compress or drop it. | Shrinks the "loop memory" the attention mechanism can latch onto. | Risky: the pruned span might contain a number or constraint needed later. |

--- 3 · PROMPTING (how the generation is not framed)

| # | Technique | How it helps | Quality risk |
|---|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| P1 | **Structural scaffolding** – require the model to fill a template: `## Hypothesis → ## Evidence → ## Inference → ## Check`. Each section must be ≤ N tokens and must not repeat the previous section's content. | Makes verbatim loops structurally harder; forces state transitions. | Over-rigidity can truncate a genuinely iterative argument. |
| P2 | **Explicit anti-loop instruction with a concrete rule** – e.g., "If you notice you are re-stating a point, write `[RESTATE → skip]` and move to the next sub-question." | Gives the model a *licensed* escape hatch rather than a vague "don't repeat." | Model may over-trigger the skip and lose nuance. |
| P3 | **Periodic self-checkpoint injection** (serving-side, see S3) – every 2 k tokens, inject: "Summarise your current state in one sentence, then continue with a *different* angle." | Resets the internal state; the summary acts as a new "anchor" for attention. | Adds tokens; the summary itself can loop if the model is deeply stuck. |
| P4 | **Few-shot "escape" exemplars** – include 1–2 short examples in the system prompt showing the model detecting a loop and pivoting. | Calibrates the model's implicit policy toward non-repetition. | Limited effect if the loop is driven by attention mechanics rather than policy. |
| P5 | **Constrained output grammar** – force the thinking to be a sequence of labelled steps with a grammar that forbids two consecutive steps with the same label. | Makes a pure verbatim loop syntactically impossible. | May feel artificial; can reduce the natural "mulling" that helps hard problems. |

--- 4 · TRAINING (how the model is learned / fine-tuned)

| # | Technique | How it helps | Quality risk |
|---|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| T1 | **RLHF / DPO with a repetition-aware reward** – reward = answer-correctness − λ · (max n-gram self-overlap in the CoT). Train the policy to internalise "don't loop." | Most robust fix: the model learns to *want* to change direction. | If λ is too high, the model learns to be terse and skip useful re-statement. Needs careful reward shaping. |
| T2 | **Auxiliary "diversity" loss** – during SFT, add a loss term that penalises cosine similarity between the hidden states at position *t* and position *t − k* for a range of k. | Directly trains the representation to avoid self-similarity over short windows. | May reduce the model's ability to legitimately re-derive a constraint. |
| T3 | **Curriculum on "stuck-then-recover" data** – collect (or synthesise) traces where the model loops, then show the *correct* continuation after the loop. Fine-tune on the recovery. | Teaches the model a concrete "what to do when stuck" policy. | Data is expensive to curate; recovery may be domain-specific. |
| T4 | **Distillation from a non-looping teacher** – use a model (or a heavily scaffolded version of the same model) that doesn't loop as the teacher; distill its soft labels. | Bakes in the teacher's attention/decoding behaviour without changing architecture. | Student inherits the teacher's blind spots; may lose capabilities the student had. |
| T5 | **Position-encoding retraining with a "forgetting" prior** – train with a modified PE that decays the influence of tokens older than *M*, so the model learns to rely on its own summary rather than raw recency. | Addresses the architectural root cause permanently. | Requires full pre-training or heavy continued pre-training; very expensive. |

--- 5 · SERVING / INFERENCE INFRASTRUCTURE (how the model is not deployed)

| # | Technique | How it helps | Quality risk |
|---|-----------|--------------|--------------|
| X1 | **Real-time n-gram loop detector** – a streaming scanner flags when a 6–10-gram repeats ≥ 3× in the current output. On trigger: (a) apply S1, (b) inject P3, or (c) early-stop and return the best partial answer. | Catches loops *as they happen* before they consume the entire budget. | False positives on legitimate repeated structure (e.g., a table). Tune thresholds per task. |
| X2 | **Dynamic budget with a "stuck" penalty** – if the detector fires, shrink the remaining token budget by 50 % and re-prompt with P3. If it fires again, terminate and return the last coherent checkpoint. | Prevents the "waste the whole budget on a loop" failure mode. | The user gets a shorter answer; may miss a correct-but-late derivation. |
| X3 | **Speculative decoding with a loop-aware verifier** – the draft model proposes tokens; the verifier (the full model) rejects any draft span that would create a 4-gram match with the last 128 tokens. | Catches loops *before* they're committed to the KV cache. | Extra compute for the verifier; the rejection criterion must be tuned to avoid killing valid text. |
| X4 | **Multi-attempt with parameter diversity** – if the first attempt loops, discard and retry with T ↑ 0.3, a different seed, or a re-phrased prompt. Keep the best non-looping attempt. | Guarantees the user gets *some* answer even if one trajectory loops. | 2–3× latency for the retry; still fails if the problem is inherently loop-prone. |
| X5 | **Client-side "progress" heartbeat** – the API returns a lightweight signal every 512 tokens ("novelty score"). The client can decide to abort and re-prompt before the budget is exhausted. | Puts the escape-hatch decision in the application layer, where it can be tuned per use-case. | Adds API surface; the novelty score must be cheap to compute. |

--- Ranking: Expected Effectiveness vs. Cost to Test I've scored each technique on two axes. **Effectiveness** = expected reduction in loop rate *without* measurable quality loss (1–5). **Cost to test** = engineering effort + GPU/compute to get a reliable A/B number (1 = trivial, 5 = multi-week training run).

| Rank | Technique (layer) | Effectiveness (1-5) | Cost to test (1-5) | Effort/Eff ratio | Notes |
|------|-------------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|-------|
| 1 | S1 – adaptive n-gram block (sampling) | 4 | 1 | ★★★★★ | One config flag + a small resample loop. Test on 200 held-out prompts in an afternoon. |
| 2 | P1 – structural scaffolding (prompting) | 3 | 1 | ★★★★★ | Edit the system prompt. Test same evening. May not help on free-form tasks. |
| 3 | X1 – real-time loop detector (serving) | 4 | 2 | ★★★★☆ | A few hundred lines of streaming code. Catches loops the sampling fix misses. |
| 4 | D1 – sliding-window + summary KV (decoding) | 4 | 3 | ★★★☆☆ | Needs a summariser call every ~4 k tokens; moderate infra work. Addresses root cause. |
| 5 | S3 – two-temperature schedule (sampling) | 3 | 2 | ★★★★☆ | Needs a cheap transition detector (entropy or a tiny classifier). |
| 6 | P3 – self-checkpoint injection (prompting) | 3 | 1 | ★★★★☆ | Trivial to add; but the summary itself can loop, so pair with X1. |
| 7 | T1 – RLHF with repetition penalty (training) | 5 | 5 | ★★☆☆☆ | Most robust long-term fix, but a full RL run + eval is weeks of GPU. |
| 8 | D2 – attention-entropy monitor (decoding) | 3 | 4 | ★★☆☆☆ | Requires hooking into the model's attention tensors; hard to A/B without model surgery. |
| 9 | X3 – loop-aware speculative verifier (serving) | 3 | 3 | ★★★☆☆ | Moderate infra; interacts with the draft model's quality. |
| 10 | T2 – auxiliary diversity loss (training) | 4 | 5 | ★★☆☆☆ | Powerful but needs a continued-pre-training budget. |
| 11 | S4 – top-p floor (sampling) | 2 | 1 | ★★★☆☆ | Cheap safety net; rarely the *primary* fix. |
| 12 | D3 – position-encoding jitter (decoding) | 3 | 4 | ★★☆☆☆ | Model surgery; hard to validate without a full eval suite. |
| 13 | X4 – multi-attempt retry (serving) | 2 | 2 | ★★★☆☆ | Safety net, not a fix; doubles latency on trigger. |
| 14 | T3 – stuck-then-recover curriculum (training) | 3 | 4 | ★★☆☆☆ | Data curation is the bottleneck; domain-dependent. |
| 15 | D4 – auxiliary "progress" head (decoding) | 3 | 5 | ★☆☆☆☆ | Needs a new training pass + a well-calibrated head; hardest to get right. |
| 16 | T5 – PE retraining with forgetting prior (training) | 4 | 5 | ★☆☆☆☆ | Most architecturally deep; most expensive. |

| 22 | T4 – distillation from non-looping teacher (training) | 3 | 4 | ★★☆☆☆ | Inherits the teacher's weaknesses; moderate training cost. |
