# Design Document: Weekly Fail-Fast Funnel for Open-Weight Model Releases

## 1. Purpose and Constraints

Each week, new open-weight model releases (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, etc.) appear. We evaluate them on **one machine** with a fixed weekly time budget. The goal is to spend the bulk of that budget on the small number of candidates that actually clear the bar, while eliminating the rest in seconds or minutes.

Hard constraints:

- **One machine, one week.** Total GPU-hours available is fixed (e.g., 40 h on a single A100-80G). Every stage must be budgeted against that.
- **Fail-fast.** A candidate that fails at stage *k* never reaches stage *k+1*.
- **Reproducible.** Every score is a function of (weights, prompt, sampling params, eval harness version). Same inputs → same outputs.

---

## 2. The Stages

Stages are ordered strictly by cost. Each stage has a single question: *"Is there a cheap, mechanical test that can eliminate this candidate?"* If yes, run it. If the candidate passes, promote it.

| Stage | Name | Budget | Cheapest disqualifying test | Promote-on evidence |
|-------|------|--------|----------------------------|---------------------|
| 0 | Triage | < 1 min, no GPU | Weights don't download; license incompatible with our use; architecture unsupported by our inference stack; parameter count / context length outside our hardware envelope | Metadata matches the requirements checklist |
| 1 | Smoke | < 5 min GPU | Model fails to load; crashes on first forward pass; outputs are token soup or repeats | 10 fixed prompts produce coherent, on-topic text (checked by a small judge model or exact-match on expected substrings) |
| 2 | Core benchmark | 15–40 min GPU | Score on a **fixed 500-question set** (MMLU-style MCQ + GSM8K-style math + a short coding set) falls below a **pre-registered floor** (e.g., 10 pts below our current production model) | Meets the floor on every sub-task |
| 3 | Application eval | 1–4 h GPU | Fails on **our own task set** (the prompts we actually serve in production, scored by a judge LLM against a pre-written rubric) below the application bar | ≥ 90 % of rubric items pass; no single task category below 70 % |
| 4 | Stress & safety | 2–6 h GPU | Adversarial / jailbreak prompts produce harmful output; long-context (> 32k) generation degrades past a threshold; repeated sampling shows variance that violates a stability band | Passes all red-team probes; context degradation within tolerance |
| 5 | Shadow deploy | 1–3 days wall-clock | Live shadow traffic shows latency regression > 20 % or quality regression on a held-out production slice | Meets SLOs; quality ≥ current model on the slice |

A candidate that reaches stage 5 is a **promotion candidate** for the fleet. Everything else is logged and retired.

### Why this ordering

The expensive tests (stage 3–5) are only meaningful if the model is *competent at all*. Stage 2's 500-question set is the single highest-leverage filter: it distinguishes "broken / toy" from "actually usable" at roughly 1 % of the cost of a full application eval. Most weekly releases die here or earlier.

---

## 3. What "Evidence Promotes a Candidate" Means Concretely

Promotion is **threshold-based, not vibes-based**. Each stage writes a structured record:

```json
{
  "model_id": "org/model-v2-70b",
  "stage": 2,
  "timestamp": "2025-07-14T09:32:00Z",
  "harness_version": "evalkit-3.2.1",
  "scores": {"mmlu": 78.4, "gsm8k": 61.0, "coding": 55.2},
  "floor":   {"mmlu": 72, "gsm8k": 55, "coding": 50},
  "verdict": "PROMOTE",
  "artifacts": ["runs/2025-07-14/model-v2-70b/stage2/"]
}
```

A candidate is promoted only when **every** sub-threshold in the record is met. There is no "it's close enough, let's give it a shot at stage 3." The thresholds are set once per quarter and versioned.

---

## 4. Avoiding Re-Testing What Is Already Known

This is the single biggest source of wasted GPU-hours in a weekly loop, because model families iterate fast (Llama 3.1 → 3.2 → 4) and a lot of the evaluation is redundant.

### 4.1 Content-addressed eval cache

Every evaluation run is keyed by a hash of:

```
key = sha256(
    model_weights_blob_id,   # from the HF repo, not the model name
    prompt_set_version,
    sampling_params,         # temperature, top_p, max_tokens
    harness_version,
    judge_model_id           # if a judge LLM is used
)
```

Before any stage runs, the pipeline checks a persistent SQLite/Postgres table (`eval_results`). If the key exists, the cached score is reused and the stage is skipped. This means:

- Re-running the weekly scan after a crash costs zero GPU.
- If a model is re-released with identical weights (renamed repo), it's a cache hit.

### 4.2 Delta evaluation for fine-tunes and distills

When a new release shares a base checkpoint (e.g., "Qwen3-32B-Instruct" is a fine-tune of "Qwen3-32B"), the base's stage-2 scores are already cached. The pipeline runs only the **delta prompts**: the subset of the eval set on which the fine-tune is expected to differ (instruction-following, formatting, refusal behaviour). This typically cuts stage-2 time by 60–80 %.

The delta set is defined per family and versioned alongside the full set.

### 4.3 Family-level short-circuits

If a model family has been evaluated three consecutive weeks and the new release is a "refresh" (same architecture, same size, incremental training), stage 1 and stage 2 use a **reduced prompt set** (100 questions instead of 500) unless the release notes claim a major training change. The full set is re-run only when the reduced set shows a > 3-point swing.

### 4.4 What is never cached

- Stage 4 (safety / adversarial) is **never** served from cache, because the adversarial set is rotated weekly and because a model that was safe last week can regress with a new fine-tune.
- Stage 5 (shadow deploy) is never cached by definition.

---

## 5. Keeping the Process Honest When a Favourite Is Failing

This is the hardest part and the part that silently breaks most eval pipelines. The risk: a model you've invested in, championed, or built your roadmap around fails stage 3. The natural response is to "try one more thing" — a different temperature, a different prompt, a second run "to confirm." Each rescue attempt is a confirmation-bias loop that burns the week's budget and delays the real decision.

### 5.1 Pre-register the criteria

Thresholds, prompt sets, judge rubrics, and sampling parameters are written into a **versioned config file** (`eval_config_2025Q3.yaml`) **before** the weekly scan begins. The pipeline reads that file; it does not accept ad-hoc overrides at run time. If you want to change a threshold, you do it for next week's scan and the change is logged with a reason.

### 5.2 Mechanical verdicts, no human in the loop at stages 0–4

Stages 0–4 are fully automated. The pipeline emits `PROMOTE` or `RETIRE` from the config. A human does not "look at the outputs and decide it's actually fine." If a human disagrees with a verdict, they file an **override ticket** that is logged, attributed, and reviewed at the weekly retro. The override does not re-run the eval with tweaked parameters; it triggers a *new* eval with a *new*, pre-registered config.

### 5.3 No re-run rescues

If a candidate fails stage 2, it is retired. There is no "run it again with temperature 0.3 instead of 0.7." The sampling parameters are part of the cache key and the config. If you believe the parameters are wrong, you change the config for next week and re-evaluate **all** candidates under the new parameters.

### 5.4 The "favourite" log

Every override, every threshold change, every "let me just look at these outputs" is written to an append-only log with the person's name and timestamp. At the weekly retro, the log is reviewed. If the same person has overridden three favourites in a row, that pattern is visible and can be discussed. The log is not punitive; it is a calibration instrument.

### 5.5 Separate the person who sets criteria from the person who runs the scan

If possible, the eval config (thresholds, prompt sets, rubrics) is owned by one person or team, and the weekly execution is owned by another. This is the cheapest structural guard against the person who loves the model also tuning the bar to let it through. On a one-machine shop this may be the same person wearing two hats on different days; the key is that the config is frozen before the scan and the scan is run mechanically.

### 5.6 A "control" candidate every week

Each weekly scan includes one **known-good** model (your current production model) and one **known-bad** model (a deliberately weak or broken checkpoint). These run through the full funnel. If the known-good fails or the known-bad passes, the harness itself is broken and **no verdicts that week are trusted**. This catches silent regressions in the eval code, the judge model, or the inference stack that would otherwise be mistaken for model quality.

---

## 6. Weekly Operating Cadence

| Day | Activity |
|-----|----------|
| Mon AM | Scan Hugging Face / release feeds. Populate the candidate list. Run stage 0 (triage) on everything. |
| Mon PM | Stage 1 (smoke) on survivors. Typically 3–8 candidates remain. |
| Tue | Stage 2 (core benchmark) on survivors. Typically 1–3 remain. |
| Wed–Thu | Stage 3 (application eval) on survivors. |
| Fri AM | Stage 4 (stress & safety) on any candidate that passed stage 3. |
| Fri PM | If a candidate passed stage 4, queue stage 5 (shadow deploy) for the following week. Write the weekly report: what was tested, what passed, what failed, any overrides. |

If no candidate reaches stage 4, the week ends with a short "no promotion" report. That is a valid and common outcome. The funnel's job is to make "nothing new is good enough" a fast, cheap conclusion rather than a three-day slog.

---

## 7. Artefacts and Tooling

- **`evalkit`** – the harness. A Python package that loads a model, runs a prompt set, scores outputs, and writes the structured record. Versioned. Pinned in the config.
- **`eval_results` DB** – persistent store of every run, keyed as in §4.1. Survives machine reboots; lives on a small SSD or network share.
- **`eval_config_YYYYQn.yaml`** – thresholds, prompt-set versions, sampling params, judge model ID. One file per quarter, reviewed at quarter boundaries.
- **`override_log.md`** – append-only, human-written, reviewed weekly.
- **Weekly report** – auto-generated from the DB: table of candidates × stages × verdicts, with links to raw run directories.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Future Work

- **Judge model drift.** The LLM judge used in stages 3–4 is itself a model that changes. When the judge is updated, all downstream scores shift. Mitigation: pin the judge version in the config; re-baseline all thresholds when the judge changes.
- **Multi-GPU or multi-machine scaling.** The design assumes one box. If a second machine is added, stages 3–4 can be parallelised across candidates, but the funnel ordering and caching keys stay the same.
- **Continuous vs. weekly.** If release cadence exceeds weekly, the triage stage (stage 0) can run daily and the rest of the funnel runs weekly on the accumulated survivors. The cache makes this cheap.

---

*Document owner: [eval team]. Review cadence: quarterly, aligned to config version bumps.*

# Fail-Fast Funnel: Weekly Evaluation of Open-Weight Model Releases

## 1. Purpose and Constraints

Each week, one or more new open-weight models appear (new releases, fine-tunes, quantised variants, architecture changes). This document defines a single-machine evaluation pipeline that **rejects the obvious failures in minutes** and spends its scarce GPU-hours only on candidates that survive every cheaper gate.

Hard constraints the design must respect:

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---|
| **One machine** | Total weekly GPU budget is fixed (assume ~40 GPU-hours). Every stage must have a hard time cap. |
| **Weekly cadence** | At most one full evaluation cycle per week. Anything that can't finish in a week is deferred, not run. |
| **Open weights** | We can download, load, and inspect the model directly. No API dependency. |
| **Fail-fast** | Stages are ordered by cost. A candidate that fails stage *k* never reaches stage *k+1*. |

The funnel is not a ranking system. It is a **gatekeeper**: each stage answers one yes/no question — *"is this model worth spending more compute on?"* — and the cheapest test that can answer "no" is the one that runs.

---

## 2. The Stages

Five stages, each with a fixed time budget, a mechanical disqualifier, and a promotion criterion. A candidate either advances or is logged as rejected with the specific evidence.

### Stage 0 — Metadata Triage
**Budget: 0 minutes of GPU. ~10 minutes of reading.**

What runs: a script pulls the model card, `config.json`, tokenizer files, and the HuggingFace / repo metadata. No model is loaded.

**Cheapest disqualifiers (checked in this order):**

1. **License.** Is the license compatible with your deployment and distribution constraints? (e.g., an "AI-Only" or research-only license disqualifies a model you need in a commercial product.) This is a string match against a maintained allow-list.
2. **Architecture / precision.** Can your hardware actually load it? If the model requires a tensor-parallel layout across 8 GPUs, or ships only in FP8 with no GGUF/AWQ variant, it's out on a single machine.
3. **Context window.** If your workload requires ≥ 32k tokens and the model's `max_position_embeddings` is 4k, disqualify.
4. **Provenance.** Is the checkpoint a verified release from the stated organisation, or an unverified re-upload? Unverified provenance → reject (this is a supply-chain check, not a quality check).

**Promotion criterion:** all four checks pass. The candidate enters the download queue.

> *Why this stage exists:* most "new releases" that appear in a week are quantised variants, LoRA adapters for models you already evaluated, or re-uploads. Stage 0 filters those out for free.

---

### Stage 1 — Loadability and Smoke Test
**Budget: 15 minutes of GPU. 5 prompts.**

What runs: download the weights, load the model into memory (or VRAM), and generate 5 completions from a fixed smoke-test prompt set:

- a one-sentence factual question with a known answer,
- a simple arithmetic problem,
- a "repeat the following exactly" instruction (tests instruction-following plumbing),
- a prompt in a non-English language,
- a prompt that should produce a short, structured output (e.g., "list 3 items as JSON").

**Cheapest disqualifiers:**

1. **Load failure.** The model doesn't load, OOMs, or the tokenizer is mismatched (garbage token IDs). → Reject.
2. **Gibberish.** Any of the 5 completions is incoherent, loops, or is entirely in the wrong language. → Reject.
3. **Instruction plumbing broken.** The "repeat exactly" prompt produces a paraphrase or ignores the format. → Reject.

**Promotion criterion:** all 5 completions are coherent, on-topic, and structurally correct. The model is *alive and talking sensibly*.

> *Why 5 prompts:* this is the minimum set that catches the three most common failure modes in open-weight releases (broken checkpoint, tokenizer mismatch, missing chat-template wiring) without spending more than a few hundred tokens of generation.

---

### Stage 2 — Fixed-Subset Calibration
**Budget: 30–60 minutes of GPU. 100–200 completions.**

What runs: a **versioned, frozen** evaluation battery. This is not a full benchmark; it is a stratified sample drawn from the benchmarks you actually care about:

| Sub-battery | Size | Source | What it catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Factual recall | 40 | MMLU / TriviaQA sample | Catastrophic knowledge gaps |
| Arithmetic / reasoning | 30 | GSM8K subset | Basic reasoning broken |
| Instruction following | 30 | IFEval / custom | Formatting and constraint adherence |
| Code generation | 20 | HumanEval subset | Code sanity |
| Summarisation / extraction | 20 | Custom task prompts | Your actual workload shape |

All prompts, the sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, max tokens), and the scoring scripts are **pinned to a version** (see §4).

**Cheapest disqualifier:** a single sub-battery scoring below a **hard floor**. The floor is set per sub-battery and is *not* the adoption threshold — it is the "is this model broken" threshold.

Example floors (tune to your domain):

- Factual recall < 25% → reject
- Arithmetic < 20% → reject
- Instruction following < 30% → reject
- Any sub-battery < 15% → reject (regardless of which one)

**Promotion criterion:** every sub-battery clears its floor. The model is *competent enough to evaluate on your real tasks*.

> *Why floors, not a single aggregate:* a model that scores 80% on factual recall but 5% on instruction following is not "average" — it is broken for your use case. Per-battery floors prevent a strong sub-score from masking a catastrophic one.

---

### Stage 3 — Task-Relevant Evaluation
**Budget: 4–8 hours of GPU. 500–2 000 completions.**

What runs: a curated set of prompts drawn from **your actual workload**. This is the stage where the evaluation stops being generic and becomes specific to your product, research task, or pipeline.

Two components:

1. **Representative sample.** 300–500 prompts sampled from production logs, user tickets, or a manually curated task set. Scored with a mix of exact-match, LLM-as-judge (a fixed, pinned judge model), and human spot-checks (you or a colleague read 20–30 outputs).
2. **A/B against the current incumbent.** The same prompts are run against the model currently in production. You get a per-prompt win/loss/tie, not just a single aggregate number.

**Disqualifier:** the candidate does not meet the **adoption threshold** you pre-registered (see §5). Concretely:

- Win rate against incumbent < 50% (i.e., it is not better than what you already have), **or**
- Any critical task category (e.g., "safety refusal," "structured output") has a win rate < 40%.

**Promotion criterion:** the candidate beats the incumbent at or above the pre-registered threshold on the representative sample, with no critical category below its floor.

> *Why A/B instead of absolute scores:* absolute benchmark scores are noisy and not calibrated to your task. "Is it better than what I already run?" is the only question that matters at this stage.

---

### Stage 4 — Robustness and Edge Cases
**Budget: 8–16 hours of GPU. 1 000–3 000 completions.**

What runs: adversarial and edge-case probes. This is the stage that catches the failures that look fine on a representative sample:

- **Long-context degradation.** Prompts with 16k, 32k, 64k tokens of context. Does quality degrade gracefully or collapse?
- **Adversarial / jailbreak probes.** A fixed set of 50–100 known jailbreak and prompt-injection templates. (Not a safety certification — just "does it have the same failure modes as the incumbent?")
- **Distribution shift.** Prompts in domains the model was likely not trained on (e.g., your niche industry terminology).
- **Consistency.** Run 20 prompts 5× each with temperature > 0. Does the model produce wildly different answers, or is it stable?
- **Latency / throughput profile.** Measure tokens/sec on your hardware. If the model is 3× slower than the incumbent with no quality gain, that's a disqualifier.

**Disqualifier:** any of the following:

- Long-context quality drops below the Stage 2 floor at your required context length.
- > 20% of adversarial probes produce a safety failure that the incumbent does not.
- Consistency check shows > 30% of repeated prompts flip the answer.
- Throughput is < 50% of the incumbent's with no quality improvement.

**Promotion criterion:** all edge-case checks pass. The candidate is **adopted** (or queued for a human sign-off, see §5).

---

### Summary Table

| Stage | GPU Time | Completions | Question Answered | Disqualifier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 – Metadata | 0 | 0 | Is it even loadable / licensed / relevant? | License, arch, context, provenance |
| 1 – Smoke | ~15 min | 5 | Is it alive and talking? | Gibberish, broken plumbing |
| 2 – Calibration | ~45 min | 100–200 | Is it competent? | Any sub-battery below hard floor |
| 3 – Task-relevant | 4–8 h | 500–2 000 | Is it better than what I have? | Win rate below pre-registered threshold |
| 4 – Robustness | 8–16 h | 1 000–3 000 | Will it break in production? | Edge-case failure, latency regression |

Total worst-case GPU time for a single candidate: ~28 hours. Realistically, most candidates die at Stage 0 or 1, so the weekly budget covers 2–4 candidates that reach Stage 3 or 4.

---

## 3. What Evidence Promotes a Candidate

Promotion is **mechanical**, not judgmental. At each stage, the promotion decision is a function of the scores against pre-registered thresholds. There is no "I think it's good enough" step.

The evidence that promotes a candidate is:

1. **The raw scores** from that stage's evaluation battery, written to a results file.
2. **The pass/fail determination** computed by the scoring script, not by a human reading the numbers.
3. **A timestamped log entry** recording: model ID, revision, stage, scores, pass/fail, and the threshold that was applied.

A human may *inspect* the evidence (read a few completions, sanity-check a score), but the **gate decision is made by the script**. This is the single most important design choice for honesty (see §5).

---

## 4. Avoiding Re-Testing What Is Already Known

The biggest waste in a weekly process is re-running an evaluation that already ran last week on the same weights. Three mechanisms prevent this:

### 4.1 Content-Addressed Caching

Every evaluation result is keyed by a tuple:

```
cache_key = hash(
    model_id,          # e.g., "org/model-name"
    revision,          # git commit or HF revision hash of the weights
    eval_suite_version # version of the prompts + scoring script
)
```

Before any stage runs, the pipeline checks the cache. If the key exists, the stage is skipped and the cached result is used. This means:

- A model that was fully evaluated last week and has not been updated → **zero GPU time** this week.
- A model with a new revision (new weights) → full re-evaluation, because the key changed.
- An eval suite update (you added 10 prompts) → only the stages whose suite version changed re-run.

The cache is a local SQLite or JSON store. No infrastructure needed.

### 4.2 Suite Versioning

The evaluation batteries (the prompt sets, scoring scripts, sampling parameters) are versioned like code. Each version has a changelog. When you update a suite:

- Bump the version.
- Old results remain valid for the old version.
- New results are computed for the new version.
- You never silently change a prompt and expect the old score to still apply.

This prevents the subtle failure mode of "I tweaked a prompt last Tuesday, so the score from last week is no longer comparable, but I didn't notice."

### 4.3 Deduplication at Stage 0

Before anything is queued, the pipeline checks:

- Has this exact `(model_id, revision)` been evaluated before? → Skip entirely.
- Is this a known quantised variant (GGUF, AWQ, GPTQ) of a base model you already evaluated? → Evaluate only the quantisation-specific checks (Stage 1 smoke + latency), skip Stages 2–4 unless the base model was a close miss.
- Is this a LoRA / adapter for a base model you already have? → Evaluate the adapter on top of the cached base, not the full model.

---

## 5. Keeping the Process Honest When a Favourite Is Failing

This is the most important section. The failure mode is not technical; it is psychological. You have a model you *want* to adopt — it's from a team you admire, it's the "next big thing," it scored well on a viral benchmark tweet. It is failing your Stage 3 evaluation. What do you do?

The design answer is: **you do nothing. The script does.**

### 5.1 Pre-Register the Thresholds

Before the weekly evaluation cycle begins, the adoption thresholds (win rate, per-category floors, latency minimums) are written down in a config file and committed. They are set based on your requirements, not on any specific model.

You may update thresholds between weeks, but:

- The update is a code change with a commit message explaining why.
- The update applies to the *next* cycle, not the current one.
- You cannot change the threshold mid-evaluation and re-run.

This makes it structurally impossible to say "well, I'll lower the bar for this one."

### 5.2 The Gate Is a Script, Not a Person

The pass/fail decision at every stage is computed by the scoring script. The script reads the scores, compares them to the thresholds, and writes `PASS` or `FAIL` to the log. A human can read the log and the raw completions, but **the human does not set the pass/fail flag**.

If you want to override, you must:

1. Write a separate override file with a written justification.
2. The override is logged alongside the script's `FAIL` verdict, so the record shows both.
3. The override is reviewed by a second person (or by you, a week later, with fresh eyes).

This does not prevent override. It makes override **visible, logged, and accountable**.

### 5.3 The Graveyard Log

Every rejected model gets an entry in a permanent log:

```
2025-07-14 | org/some-model v2.1 | REJECTED at Stage 2
  Factual recall: 22% (floor: 25%)
  Arithmetic: 41% (floor: 20%) ✓
  Instruction following: 38% (floor: 30%) ✓
  Reason: factual recall below floor
```

This log is append-only. You cannot delete an entry. You cannot re-run a rejected model without a new revision or a new suite version (which changes the cache key and creates a new entry).

The graveyard log serves two purposes:

- **It makes re-testing a favourite expensive.** To re-evaluate a model you rejected last month, you must explain why the old rejection no longer applies. The log makes that explanation visible.
- **It calibrates your expectations.** After 20 weeks, you have a record of what actually passed and what didn't, and you can see whether your thresholds are too strict or too loose.

### 5.4 Separate Evaluation from Adoption

The person who runs the evaluation pipeline is not the person who makes the adoption decision (or, if it's the same person, the roles are separated in time). The evaluation produces a **report**: scores, pass/fail per stage, comparison to incumbent, edge-case findings. The adoption decision is a separate step that reads the report.

This separation means that the evaluation is not shaped by the desire to adopt. You are not tuning the eval to make the favourite pass. The eval runs the same way for every model, and the report is what it is.

### 5.5 The "One More Test" Rule

A common rationalisation: "The model failed instruction-following, but maybe it's a fluke. Let me run 50 more prompts on just that sub-battery."

The rule: **you may run one additional probe battery for a failed sub-battery, but the probe battery is pre-defined and versioned.** You cannot write new prompts on the fly to "see if it works better." The probe is a fixed set of 50 additional prompts from the same distribution, and the combined score (original + probe) is compared to the same threshold.

This allows for variance in a small sample without allowing for confirmation-seeking.

---

## 6. Operational Cadence

A weekly cycle looks like this:

| Day | Activity |
|---|---|
| **Monday** | Scan for new releases (HF trending, org announcements, arXiv). Run Stage 0 on all candidates. Queue survivors. |
| **Tuesday** | Run Stage 1 (smoke) on all queued candidates. Reject failures. |
| **Wednesday** | Run Stage 2 (calibration) on survivors. Reject failures. |
| **Thursday** | Run Stage 3 (task-relevant) on survivors. This is the expensive day. |
| **Friday** | Run Stage 4 (robustness) on the 1–2 survivors. Write the weekly report. Make adoption decisions. Update the graveyard log. |

If the GPU budget is exhausted before Friday, the remaining candidates are deferred to next week. The funnel does not skip stages to save time.

---

## 7. What This Document Does Not Cover

- **Model fine-tuning or distillation.** This is an evaluation pipeline, not a training pipeline. If a candidate is close but not quite good enough, the answer is "reject and fine-tune," not "lower the threshold."
- **Safety certification.** Stage 4's adversarial probes are a regression check, not a safety audit. If your deployment requires a formal safety evaluation, that is a separate, more expensive process.
- **Multi-model routing.** This document evaluates models one at a time. Deciding whether to route different tasks to different models is a downstream problem.
- **Continuous monitoring.** This is a weekly gate. Once a model is adopted, monitoring its quality in production is a separate system.

---

## 8. Implementation Notes

- **Orchestration:** a single Python script (or a small Makefile / Snakemake DAG) that runs stages in sequence, checks the cache before each stage, and writes results to SQLite. No cluster, no queue, no orchestration framework. One machine, one process.
- **Scoring:** exact-match and regex for structured tasks; a pinned judge model (a small, fixed model you run locally) for open-ended tasks. The judge model is versioned and never changed mid-cycle.
- **Prompts and suites:** stored in a git repo. The `eval_suite_version` in the cache key is the git commit hash of the suite repo.
- **The graveyard log:** a single Markdown or CSV file in the repo. Append-only by convention; enforced by a pre-commit hook that rejects deletions.
- **The report:** auto-generated from the SQLite results. One page per candidate. Stamped with the suite version and the model revision.

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Model Architecture

For triage (priority ranking, not diagnosis), you want a system that's fast, calibrated, and explainable. A practical stack:

**Backbone: EfficientNet-B4 or ViT-B/16 (patch size 16)**
- For chest X-rays: a dual-branch model. Branch 1 is a CNN (EfficientNet-B4, 21M params) for local texture/edge features. Branch 2 is a Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16, ~86M params) for global context. Fuse via a 256-dim concat + 2-layer MLP head.
- For CT (chest, head, abdomen): use a 3D backbone. **3D ViT with patch size 8×8×8** on 128³ volumes, or a **3D ResNet-50** if your GPU budget is tight. For multi-slice CT, you can also use a 2D model on axial slices with a slice-selection module (a lightweight CNN that scores each slice for relevance, then feeds the top-N slices to the classifier).

**Triage head (not diagnosis):**
- Output: a continuous urgency score in [0, 1] (e.g., "probability this study contains a finding that requires action within 1 hour vs. routine").
- Train with **ordinal regression** (CORN loss or ordinal cross-entropy) if your labels are discrete urgency tiers (STAT / Urgent / Routine / Delayed). This preserves the ordering constraint that plain softmax ignores.
- Add a **calibration layer** (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) trained on a held-out set. Triage is only useful if the score is well-calibrated — a model that says "0.92" should actually mean 92% of such studies get escalated.

**Multi-modal fusion (optional but high-value):**
- Concatenate the imaging embedding with structured metadata (age, sex, clinical indication, ordering physician, modality, body part) via a small MLP. The metadata alone carries significant triage signal (a "ground-glass opacity, 82yo, PE protocol" is a different urgency than "routine follow-up, 34yo").

**Why not a giant foundation model?** For triage you don't need diagnostic granularity. A 100M-param model that runs in <80ms per study on a single A100 is the sweet spot. You're processing *every* study in the queue, so latency and throughput matter more than top-1 accuracy.

## 2. Training Pipeline

**Data:**
- Source: your own PACS archive (DICOM) plus public datasets for pretraining (NIH ChestX-ray14, RSNA, CT-RATE for chest CT, TCIA for multi-organ CT).
- Labels: this is the hard part. Triage labels are rarely explicitly stored. You reconstruct them from:
  - Final radiologist report (NLP extraction of findings → map to urgency via a curated lexicon or a fine-tuned clinical NER model).
  - Turnaround-time logs (time from study completion to report sign-off; studies reported in <30 min were likely urgent).
  - ED disposition (admission, ICU transfer, return to ED).
- Expect to get 50k–500k labeled studies from a multi-year archive. Use **semi-supervised learning** (FixMatch or a pseudo-labeling loop) to exploit the remaining unlabeled archive.

**Augmentation:**
- 2D: random affine, elastic deformation, intensity jitter, Gaussian noise, CutOut.
- 3D: random rotation ±15°, z-axis flip, patch dropout, CT intensity normalization (HU windowing augmentation — train the model to be invariant to window/level settings).

**Training details:**
- Framework: PyTorch + Lightning. Mixed precision (FP16/BF16).
- Optimizer: AdamW, lr=2e-4 with cosine schedule, warmup 5 epochs.
- Batch size: 64 for 2D, 16 for 3D CT.
- Validation: **stratified by body part, modality, and urgency tier**. Report AUROC *and* sensitivity at fixed specificity (e.g., "sensitivity at 95% specificity" — you want to catch the STAT cases even if you over-triage some routine ones).
- Cross-validation: 5-fold, but also a **temporal split** (train on 2019–2023, test on 2024) to detect distribution drift.

## 3. PACS Integration & Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific about the integration pattern:

**DICOM workflow:**
- The PACS (GE, Philips, Siemens, or open-source Orthanc) stores DICOM objects. You do **not** pull images on demand. Instead, hook into the **DICOM Store/Retrieve** flow:
  - When a modality (CT scanner, CR/DR) sends a study to the PACS via **DICOM C-STORE**, the PACS fires a **DICOM DIMSE event** or an HL7 **ORU^OBS** / **ADT^A04** message.
  - Your triage service subscribes to these events. The cleanest pattern: deploy a **DICOM gateway / VNA (Vendor Neutral Archive) front-end** that the modalities send to. The VNA forwards to the PACS *and* publishes a message to a queue (RabbitMQ, Kafka, or even a simple PostgreSQL NOTIFY) that your inference service consumes.

**Concrete deployment topology:**

```
[Modality] --DICOM C-STORE--> [DICOM Gateway / VNA]
                                   |
                          (1) forward to PACS
                          (2) publish study UID + metadata to Kafka topic
                                   |
                                   v
                          [Triage Inference Service]
                          (FastAPI, pulls DICOM from PACS via
                           DICOMweb QIDO-RS + WADO-RS,
                           decodes to numpy, runs model)
                                   |
                                   v
                          [HL7 FHIR Server]
                          (POSTs a DiagnosticReport
                           or Observation resource with
                           the urgency score)
                                   |
                                   v
                          [RIS / Ordering System]
                          (flags the study in the
                           radiologist's worklist)
```

**DICOMweb is your friend.** Rather than raw DICOM DIMSE (which requires a DICOM toolkit like dcm4che, pydicom + pynetdicom, or Orthanc), use **DICOMweb**:
- **QIDO-RS** (query) to find studies by accession number, patient ID, modality.
- **WADO-RS** (retrieve) to pull the actual pixel data as JPEG2000, JPEG-LS, or uncompressed.
- Orthanc has a built-in DICOMweb plugin. If you're on a commercial PACS, check for DICOMweb support or deploy Orthanc as a sidecar.

**Inference service specifics:**
- Language: Python (FastAPI) or C++/Rust if you need sub-50ms latency.
- Model serving: **TensorRT** (NVIDIA) or **ONNX Runtime** for the inference graph. Quantize to FP16 or INT8.
- Hardware: 1× NVIDIA A100 or 2× A10 for a busy hospital. For a 3D CT model, you'll want the A100. For 2D CXR, a T4 or even an L4 is fine.
- Throughput target: a busy ED does ~200–400 CTs/day and ~500–1000 CXRs/day. You need to clear the queue in <5 min per study to be useful for STAT triage.
- Run as a **Kubernetes Deployment** with HPA (horizontal pod autoscaling) keyed on Kafka consumer lag. Each pod runs one GPU.

**HL7 FHIR / RIS integration:**
- The triage score needs to land in the radiologist's worklist. Two paths:
  1. **HL7v2 ORU^OBS** message to the RIS (legacy but universal).
  2. **FHIR DiagnosticReport / Observation** resource to a FHIR server (Epic, Cerner, or open-source HAPI FHIR). The RIS subscribes and flags the study.
- Include the model's **attention map / Grad-CAM heatmap** as a rendered PNG, stored as a FHIR ImagingStudy with a secondary DICOM object. Radiologists will not trust a score they can't see *why*.

## 4. Operational & Regulatory Considerations

- **FDA / CE marking:** A triage tool that changes workflow (STAT vs. routine) is a **Class II medical device** in the US (510(k) required) and **Class IIa** in the EU (MDR). If it's purely a "second reader" assist that doesn't alter the worklist, you may fall under a different classification, but be careful — if it reorders the queue, it's a device.
- **HIPAA / GDPR:** DICOM images contain PHI. Keep inference inside your VPC/on-prem. Do not send pixel data to a public cloud API. If you use a cloud GPU, use a HIPAA-BA-covered region (AWS us-east-1 with BAA, Azure Government).
- **Model monitoring:** Track the triage score distribution weekly. Alert if the mean score drifts (scanner firmware update, new protocol, new patient population). Retrain quarterly.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** The AI flags, the radiologist decides. Log every override (AI said STAT, radiologist said routine) and feed it back as a hard negative/positive for retraining.

## 5. What I'd Actually Build First

A 2D chest X-ray triage model (pneumonia, PE signs, pneumothorax, effusion) as a **proof of concept**:
1. Orthanc PACS + DICOMweb plugin in a Docker Compose stack.
2. EfficientNet-B4 trained on your archive + NIH/RSNA data, ordinal head, 4 urgency tiers.
3. FastAPI inference service, single T4 GPU, <100ms per image.
4. Kafka queue between PACS event and inference.
5. HL7v2 ORU^OBS to your RIS.
6. Grad-CAM heatmap rendered and stored as a secondary DICOM object.

Get that running end-to-end on a shadow mode (AI scores every study but doesn't touch the worklist) for 3–6 months. Measure sensitivity/specificity against actual radiologist triage decisions. Then flip it on. Expand to CT and 3D models after the pipeline is proven.

The model is maybe 20% of the engineering effort. The PACS integration, DICOM decoding edge cases (multi-frame, non-standard transfer syntaxes, corrupted studies), HL7 message parsing, and the clinical workflow change management are the other 80%. Budget accordingly.

# AI Triage for Radiology: Architecture, Training, and PACS Deployment

## 1. Problem Framing

"Triage" in radiology means **prioritizing and routing studies**, not diagnosis. Concretely, the system answers:

- **Urgency scoring**: Is this a 10-minute-read (massive PE, subarachnoid hemorrhage) or a 2-hour-read (routine knee)?
- **Findings flagging**: "Possible pneumothorax, right apical" surfaced to the radiologist before they open the study.
- **Routing**: Chest CT → thoracic subspecialist; lumbar spine → musculoskeletal.
- **Completeness check**: Missing views, poor contrast timing, motion artifact.

This is a **multi-task, multi-modality classification + detection** problem, not a single binary classifier.

---

## 2. Model Architecture

### 2a. Per-Modality Backbones

Don't build one monolith. Build **per-modality encoders** feeding a shared triage head.

| Modality | Backbone | Input | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chest / CT (axial) | **ViT-L/16** or **Swin-L** | 224×224 patches, 128 slices → sampled to 32–64 | Pretrained on ImageNet-22k; fine-tuned on CT |
| Chest X-ray | **EfficientNet-B4** or **ResNet-50** | 224×224, 2 views (PA + lateral) | Single-view, cheap to serve |
| MRI (brain, spine) | **3D Swin-Transformer** or **nnU-Net** encoder | 128×128×96 volumes | Use 3D convs or patchified 3D ViT |
| Mammography | **EfficientNet-B4** | 224×224, 4 views | |
| Ultrasound | **Video-Swin** or **TimeSformer** | 32-frame clips | |

**Key design choice: slice sampling for CT/MRI.** You don't feed all 500+ slices. Use a **slice-selection network** (a lightweight 1D CNN over the intensity profile of the volume) to pick the 32–64 most informative slices, then feed those to the 2D ViT. This is what Google's and Aidoc's pipelines do and it cuts inference cost ~10×.

### 2b. Shared Triage Head

```
[modality-specific encoder]
        ↓
   [CLS token / global pool]  →  768-d vector
        ↓
   [Linear 768 → 256]
   [LayerNorm → GELU]
        ↓
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Task heads (all share the 256-d trunk): │
   │  • Urgency: 4-class (routine → STAT)     │
   │  • Findings: multi-label, ~50 classes    │
   │  • Routing: subspecialty classifier       │
   │  • QA flags: motion / truncation / etc.  │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Train with a **multi-task loss**: `L = λ₁·CE_urgency + λ₂·BCE_findings + λ₃·CE_routing + λ₄·BCE_qa`. Tune λ per task; findings usually dominate.

### 2c. Optional: Detection Head for Localization

For "where is the pneumothorax," add a **DETR** or **RT-DETR** head on top of the ViT backbone. Output bounding boxes + labels. This is what surfaces a visual flag on the image in the viewer.

### 2d. Ensembling / Calibration

- Train **3–5 models with different data augmentations and seeds**, ensemble at inference (average logits).
- Apply **temperature scaling** on the urgency head so the 4-class probabilities are calibrated (important for threshold-based STAT escalation).
- Keep a **per-modality, per-finding confusion matrix** in your monitoring dashboard.

---

## 3. Training Pipeline

### Data

- **Source**: De-identified DICOM from your PACS (see §4). You need DICOM *metadata* (modality, body part, laterality, acquisition protocol) as features alongside the pixels.
- **Labels**: Radiologist read reports (structured if you have C-CODes / RadLex, free-text otherwise). For free text, run a **RadNER** (radiology named-entity recognition) model — e.g., a fine-tuned BioBERT on RadLex — to extract findings. This is the single biggest bottleneck; budget real radiologist time for gold-standard labeling on a 5–10k study subset.
- **Scale**: Aim for ≥ 50k studies per modality for the encoder pretrain, ≥ 5k labeled per finding class.
- **Splits**: Split by **patient**, not by study, to avoid data leakage (same patient appears in multiple studies).

### Training Loop

```
1. Pretrain encoder on large unlabeled DICOM corpus
   (self-supervised: MAE / DINOv2 on patches, or 3D SimCLR for volumes)

2. Fine-tune encoder + triage head on labeled data
   - AdamW, lr=1e-4 (encoder) / 1e-3 (head), cosine schedule
   - Mixup + RandAugment for 2D; elastic deformation + random
     slice dropout for 3D
   - Class-balanced focal loss for findings (pneumothorax is rare)

3. Train slice-selection net jointly (end-to-end) or in a
   separate stage

4. Calibration: temperature scaling on a held-out 5% set
```

Use **PyTorch + MONAI** (for 3D transforms and DICOM I/O) or **NVIDIA Clara** if you're on DGX hardware. MONAI's `DecathlonDataset` handles DICOM → NIfTI conversion cleanly.

### Validation

- Report **per-finding AUC, sensitivity @ fixed specificity (e.g., 95% spec → what's the sensitivity?)**.
- For urgency: report **time-to-detection** in a simulated queue. "STAT cases flagged within 2 min of upload" is the metric that matters clinically.
- **External validation** on a second hospital's data before any clinical use.

---

## 4. PACS Deployment

This is where most projects die. Be specific.

### 4a. DICOM Integration

You have three integration points, and you should use **all three**:

**1. DICOMweb (the primary path)**
- Your PACS must expose **DICOMweb QIDO-RS** (query) and **WADO-RS** (retrieve). Most modern PACS (GE eNet, Siemens Syngo, Agfa IMPAX, AWS HealthImaging) support this.
- Your triage service subscribes to a **DICOMweb STOW-RS** endpoint or, better, the PACS pushes **DICOMweb transactions** to your service via a callback.
- If your PACS is older and only speaks DICOM over TCP (C-STORE), deploy a **DICOM gateway / VNA** (e.g., **Orthanc**, **dcm4chee**, or **AWS HealthImaging Archive**) that accepts C-STORE and exposes DICOMweb to your AI service.

```
Modality (CT scanner)
    │  DICOM C-STORE (TCP 104)
    ▼
  PACS / VNA  (Orthanc or dcm4chee)
    │  DICOMweb WADO-RS  (HTTPS)
    │  + HL7v2 ADT / ORM messages
    ▼
  Triage AI Service
    │  DICOMweb STOW-RS (write back AI results as
    │  DICOM SR / Secondary Capture)
    ▼
  PACS  →  Radiologist workstation (VNA viewer)
```

**2. HL7v2 / FHIR for clinical context**
- Subscribe to **HL7v2 ORM^O01** (order) and **ADT^A01/A04** (admission) messages via your integration engine (Mirth Connect / Rhapsody). This gives you patient demographics, ordering physician, clinical indication, and urgency flag from the ordering system — all features for the triage model.
- If you're on FHIR, subscribe to **Bundle** resources and **Subscription** (synchronous or webhook) for `ImagingStudy` and `DiagnosticReport` resources.

**3. DICOM SR write-back**
- When the model flags findings, write a **DICOM Structured Report** (or a **DICOM Secondary Capture** with the annotated image) back into the PACS so it appears in the radiologist's reading queue. Use **pydicom** to construct the SR with RadLex-coded findings.

### 4b. Serving Stack

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DICOMweb API (FastAPI / Flask)                        │
│  - POST /studies  (accepts DICOMweb multipart)          │
│  - GET  /studies/{uid}/triage                          │
│  - POST /studies/{uid}/sr  (write back SR)             │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DICOM→Tensor pipeline (MONAI / dcm4chee)              │
│  - Parse DICOM, apply rescale, resample to model grid  │
│  - Slice selection for CT/MRI                          │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Inference (Triton Inference Server or TorchServe)     │
│  - ViT-L encoder + triage head, FP16 / INT8            │
│  - Batch size 1 (studies arrive one at a time)         │
│  - Target: < 5 s per study on 1× A10G / T4            │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Triage logic + queue management                        │
│  - Urgency score → priority queue (Redis / RabbitMQ)   │
│  - STAT → push notification to on-call radiologist     │
│  - Routing → assign to subspecialty queue              │
│  - Write DICOM SR back to PACS                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Hardware**: A single **NVIDIA A10G (24 GB)** or **T4 (16 GB)** handles the ViT-L encoder at FP16 for one study in ~2–4 s. You don't need an A100 for triage. If you're doing 3D CT with 64 slices, budget ~8 s. Run on **Kubernetes** with a GPU node pool; autoscale on queue depth.

### 4c. Orthanc as a Practical Starting Point

If you're building this in a hospital that has a legacy PACS, **Orthanc** is the pragmatic choice:

- Open-source DICOM server, speaks DICOM C-STORE, DICOMweb, and HL7v2.
- Python plugin (`orthanc-python`) lets you hook a callback when a new study arrives.
- In the callback, pull the DICOM via the Orthanc REST API, run your model, write the SR back.
- It's not a production PACS, but as a **VNA / DICOM gateway** in front of the PACS, it's battle-tested.

### 4d. Latency & SLA

- **STAT studies** (the whole point of triage): model inference must complete within **60 seconds** of the study landing in the PACS.
- **Routine studies**: within **5 minutes**.
- Implement a **timeout fallback**: if the model hasn't returned in 90 s, the study goes to the normal queue unflagged. Never block the reading queue on AI.

---

## 5. Regulatory & Operational

- **FDA / CE**: Triage as a **decision-support** tool (not autonomous) is typically Class II (FDA 510(k)) or Class IIa (CE). You need a **clinical evaluation** with a prospective study. Start the regulatory conversation before you build, not after.
- **HIPAA / GDPR**: DICOM de-identification (PS3.15 Annex E, basic profile minimum) before data leaves the hospital. If training on-prem, keep it on-prem.
- **Model monitoring**: Track **drift** in input distributions (new scanner, new protocol) and **output drift** (urgency score distribution). Alert if the STAT rate shifts > 2σ from baseline.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: The AI flags; the radiologist decides. Log every flag and every override. This is both a regulatory requirement and your retraining data source.

---

## 6. Realistic Timeline

| Phase | Duration | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Data pipeline + DICOMweb integration | 4–6 wk | Orthanc/gateway + DICOM→tensor pipeline |
| Encoder pretrain + triage head train | 6–8 wk | v0 model, internal eval |
| Radiologist labeling (5–10k studies) | 8–12 wk (parallel) | Gold-standard labels |
| Integration with PACS + queue + SR write-back | 4–6 wk | End-to-end in a shadow mode |
| Shadow mode (AI runs, humans ignore) | 4–6 wk | Sensitivity/specificity on real queue |
| Prospective clinical study + regulatory | 6–12 mo | FDA 510(k) / CE submission |

A realistic path to a **clinically deployable triage tool** is **18–24 months** from kickoff, assuming you have PACS DICOMweb support and radiologist time.

---

If you want, I can go deeper on any of these: the slice-selection network, the RadNER labeling pipeline, Triton model config for the ViT, or the Orthanc callback code. What's your current PACS stack and modality focus?

# Mechanical Devices Inventory System — Architecture & Sprint Plan

---

## 1. System Connection Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        CLIENT (Browser)                                │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  React SPA (Vite)                                                │  │
│  │  • React Router (routes)                                         │  │
│  │  • TanStack Query (data fetching / caching)                      │  │
│  │  • Zustand (auth state, UI state)                                │  │
│  │  • Axios instance (JWT interceptor, refresh-token rotation)      │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  HTTPS (TLS 1.3)
                                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    API LAYER  (Node.js 20 LTS)                        │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Express 4.x                                                     │  │
│  │  • helmet (security headers)                                     │  │
│  │  • express-rate-limit (brute-force protection)                   │  │
│  │  • cors (origin whitelist)                                       │  │
│  │  • Zod middleware (request validation)                           │  │
│  │  • JWT middleware (access + refresh token verification)          │  │
│  │  • RBAC middleware (role → permission matrix)                    │  │
│  │  • Audit-log middleware (who/what/when)                          │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Service Layer (business logic, isolated per domain)             │  │
│  │  • AuthService          • InventoryService                       │  │
│  │  • BulkUpdateService    • AdminSchemaService                     │  │
│  │  • AuditService         • UserService                            │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Data Access Layer                                              │  │
│  │  • Knex.js (query builder + migrations)                         │  │
│  │  • pg (PostgreSQL driver, connection pool)                      │  │
│  │  • Repository pattern (one repo per aggregate)                  │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  TCP / pg protocol (TLS)
                                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PostgreSQL 16                                       │
│  • Users table (id, email, password_hash, role, created_at, …)        │
│  • Devices table (id, name, reference, quantity, metadata JSONB, …)   │
│  • Audit_Log table (id, user_id, action, entity, payload, ts)        │
│  • Refresh_Tokens table (hashed token, user_id, expires_at)          │
│  • Permissions / Roles tables (for dynamic RBAC)                      │
│  • Row-Level Security (RLS) policies per role                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key architectural decisions

| Concern | Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| API style | REST with versioned routes (`/api/v1/…`) | Simple, cacheable, easy to evolve |
| Auth | JWT access (15 min) + rotating refresh (7 d) stored httpOnly cookie | Stateless horizontal scaling; refresh rotation detects theft |
| ORM / query | **Knex.js** over Sequelize | SQL-first, no magic, easy to add RLS & raw perf tweaks |
| Validation | **Zod** schemas shared FE/BE | Single source of truth, runtime + TS types |
| RBAC | Middleware chain + Postgres **Row-Level Security** | Defense-in-depth: app-layer AND DB-layer enforcement |
| Bulk ops | Transactional batch with `COPY` or `UNNEST` upsert | Avoids N round-trips; atomic per batch |
| Schema mgmt (admin) | Knex migrations + a guarded `/api/v1/admin/schema` route | Admin can add/drop columns via a *whitelisted* migration runner; never raw SQL from client |
| Horizontal scale | Stateless API behind Nginx/ALB; PgBouncer in front of Postgres | Add nodes without session stickiness |

---

## 2. Helper Code Libraries (BOM)

### Backend (Node.js)
| Library | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `express` | HTTP framework |
| `knex` + `pg` | Query builder & Postgres driver |
| `jsonwebtoken` | Sign / verify JWTs |
| `bcrypt` | Password hashing (cost 12) |

### Key Architectural Decisions

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **JWT (access 15 min) + Refresh Token (7 d, rotated)** | Stateless API scale; refresh tokens stored hashed in DB for revocation |
| **RBAC via permission matrix, not role checks in controllers** | Single source of truth; easy to add roles without touching route code |
| **Sequelize ORM + raw SQL for admin schema ops** | Type-safe CRUD; raw SQL needed for `ALTER TABLE` / dynamic fields |
| **pgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode** | Handles thousands of connections from Node cluster workers |
| **BullMQ (Redis-backed) for bulk updates** | Offloads long-running bulk ops; retries, progress tracking |
| **Audit log table** | Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE records who, what, when, old→new values |
| **PostgreSQL Row-Level Security** | Defense-in-depth: even if app-layer RBAC is bypassed, DB enforces |

| 4.8 | Build `SchemaService`: `addField(table, name, type, constraints)`, `removeField(table, name)`, `addEntity(name, fields[])`, `removeEntity(name)` |
| 4.9 | **Security:** SchemaService validates identifiers against a whitelist regex, wraps in `sequelize.query()` with **no user input in raw SQL** (parameterized); logs every schema change to `audit_logs` |
| 4.10 | API routes: `POST/DELETE /api/admin/schema/entities`, `POST/DELETE /api/admin/schema/fields` — Admin only |
| 4.11 | React **Admin → Schema Manager** page: visual form to add/remove fields on `devices` table; shows current schema; confirmation dialog for destructive ops |
| 4.12 | Add **recovery mechanism**: before any schema change, snapshot the `information_schema` state; provide `POST /api/admin/schema/rollback` |
| 4.13 | Integration tests: bulk update of 10k rows completes with correct progress; admin adds a field → it appears in API responses; non-admin gets 403 |

**Definition of Done:** Staff bulk-uploads a CSV and sees live progress; Admin adds a "warranty_date" field to devices and it immediately appears in the UI; all destructive schema ops are logged and reversible.

---

### **TICKET 5 — Security Hardening, Performance & Production Readiness**
**Goal:** Harden the application for production: security audit, performance tuning, observability, and deployment.

| # | Task |
|---|---|
| 5.1 | Run `npm audit` + `trivy` (container scan) + `snyk` on both apps; fix all critical/high CVEs |
| 5.2 | Add **CSP headers** via Helmet; configure Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy |
| 5.3 | Implement **input sanitization** layer: strip HTML, validate all params server-side; test with OWASP Top 10 payloads (SQLi, XSS, NoSQLi) |
| 5.4 | Add **audit log viewer** page (Admin + Staff): filterable table of all mutations with diff view |
| 5.5 | Implement **structured logging** (Winston JSON): every request logs `{ requestId, userId, role, method, path, status, durationMs }`; correlate via `X-Request-Id` header |
| 5.6 | Add **database indexes**: composite index on `devices(name, reference)`, index on `users(email)`, GIN index on audit log for JSONB search |
| 5.7 | Enable **pgBouncer** in transaction-pooling mode; configure Sequelize `pool` settings (`max: 20, idle: 10`); load-test with `k6` (target: p95 < 200 ms at 500 RPS) |
| 5.8 | Add **Redis caching** for read-heavy endpoints (`GET /api/devices` list, device detail) with 60 s TTL; invalidate cache on any mutation |
| 5.9 | Implement **Circuit Breaker** (opossum) around Redis and DB calls; graceful degradation |
| 5.10 | Add **health-check endpoints**: `/api/health` (liveness), `/api/health/ready` (DB + Redis connectivity) for orchestrator probes |
| 5.11 | Write **load test** script (k6): simulate 100 concurrent users doing register → login → list → update; document results |
| 5.12 | Create **deployment runbook**: env var checklist, DB migration procedure (`sequelize-cli db:migrate`), rollback steps, backup/restore (pg_dump + Redis RDB) |
| 5.13 | Add **automated backups**: nightly `pg_dump` to S3/GCS with 30-day retention; test restore quarterly |
| 5.14 | Final **penetration test checklist**: verify all 12 OWASP Top 10 mitigations are in place; document findings |
| 5.15 | Tag release `v1.0.0`; deploy to staging; run full E2E suite (Playwright); sign off |

**Definition of Done:** All security checks pass; p95 latency < 200 ms under load; backups tested; deployment runbook complete; production deploy successful.

---

## 5. Sprint Timeline at a Glance

```
Sprint 1  ──►  TICKET 1  (Infra & Scaffolding)
Sprint 2  ──►  TICKET 2  (Auth & RBAC)
Sprint 3  ──►  TICKET 3  (Inventory CRUD)
Sprint 4  ──►  TICKET 4  (Bulk Ops & Admin)
Sprint 5  ──►  TICKET 5  (Hardening & Production)
```

Each sprint is **2 weeks**. Tickets are strictly sequential because each builds on the previous (auth before CRUD, CRUD before admin schema ops). Within a ticket, tasks are ordered by dependency.

---

> **A note on the "admin manages DB fields" requirement:** This is the highest-risk feature in the system. The SchemaService (Ticket 4, tasks 4.8–4.12) deliberately uses **whitelisted identifiers + parameterized queries + snapshot/rollback** rather than passing raw user input into `ALTER TABLE` strings. I strongly recommend pairing this with a **staging approval flow** (admin proposes a schema change → it's queued → a second admin approves) before it executes in production.

# Reducing Verbatim Repetition Loops in Long-Thinking Models

## Strategies by Intervention Layer

### 1. Sampling

| Strategy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Adaptive n-gram penalty** | Apply a repetition penalty only *after* a loop is detected (e.g., the same 8–16-token window appears twice), rather than uniformly. Avoids the quality cost of penalising legitimate re-use of phrases like "therefore" or "in other words." |
| **Frequency-penalised top-k** | Track token frequencies over the last *k* tokens; when a token's frequency crosses a threshold, drop it from the candidate set. Cheap to implement in the sampler, but risks hurting structured reasoning that legitimately reuses vocabulary. |
| **Temperature annealing on loop trigger** | Keep temperature low during normal reasoning (for precision) but bump it sharply the instant a loop detector fires, so the model is forced onto a novel path. |
| **Speculative-decode rejection** | If you already run a draft model, treat a verbatim repeat of a previously emitted span as a rejection signal and resample from the target model with a perturbed seed. |

### 2. Decoding

| Strategy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Sliding-window loop detector + forced continuation** | Maintain a hash of the last *N* tokens. When the current window matches an earlier window (exact or near-exact via MinHash/SimHash), inject a short system-level nudge ("You have restated this analysis. Proceed to the next step.") and continue. |
| **Checkpoint-and-rollback** | Snapshot the KV-cache every *m* tokens. On loop detection, roll back to the last checkpoint and resample with a different seed or slightly perturbed logits. |
| **Progress-aware early stop** | Train a lightweight classifier (or use a PRM) that scores each new span for *novelty* vs. the prior context. When novelty stays near zero for *k* consecutive spans, terminate the thinking phase and force a final-answer generation. |
| **Best-of-n with loop filter** | Decode *n* candidates in parallel (or sequentially with different seeds); discard any that contain a verbatim loop; return the best survivor. Trades latency for reliability. |

### 3. Prompting

| Strategy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Structured scaffold** | Force the thinking into numbered sections or a template (Hypothesise → Test → Conclude → Next). Verbatim repetition is structurally harder when each slot expects *new* content. |
| **"Do not re-derive" instruction** | Explicit system-prompt line: *"If you have already established a fact or sub-result, reference it by label rather than re-deriving it."* Weak alone, but compounds with the scaffold. |
| **Periodic self-check injection** | Every *k* tokens, the harness appends a meta-prompt: *"Summarise what you have NOT yet covered. Continue with that."* Forces the model to re-orient. |
| **Few-shot non-repetitive exemplars** | Include 1–2 exemplars in the system prompt showing a model that labels sub-results (`[S1]`, `[S2]`) and then references them, rather than re-explaining. |

### 4. Training

| Strategy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **DPO / preference pairs on loops** | Collect (looping trace, non-looping trace) pairs from the model's own outputs. Train a DPO objective that penalises verbatim repetition. Cheap relative to RL; can be done on a subset of the base model. |
| **Process Reward Model (PRM) with a novelty signal** | Train a PRM that, in addition to correctness, scores whether each step advances the reasoning. Use it as a dense reward in RL so the model is shaped to avoid re-derivation *during* generation, not just at the end. |
| **SFT on curated progressive traces** | Filter the SFT corpus to remove traces with verbatim loops; augment with traces that explicitly label and reference sub-results. Cheap if you already have a large trace corpus. |
| **RL with a repetition-shaped reward** | Add a term to the RL reward that is proportional to the n-gram overlap between the current span and the prior context. The model learns to avoid loops as a native behaviour. Most effective but most expensive. |
| **Distillation from a non-looping oracle** | If a different architecture (e.g., a non-CoT model, or a model with a different tokeniser) rarely loops, distill its reasoning style. |

### 5. Serving / Infrastructure

| Strategy | Idea |
|---|---|
| **Streaming loop-detection middleware** | A thin layer between the model and the user that watches the token stream, detects a repeat, and either (a) truncates the thinking and forces a final answer, or (b) silently re-prompts with a "continue differently" nudge. Zero model changes. |
| **Adaptive token budget** | Allocate the thinking budget dynamically: if the loop detector fires, shrink the remaining budget and append "Conclude now with the best answer you have." Prevents the model from burning 10k tokens on a loop. |
| **Multi-attempt with diversity seeds** | At the serving layer, run the request 2–3× with different seeds. Return the first (or best-scored) non-looping answer. Simple, parallelisable, no model changes. |
| **Request re-routing** | If a loop is detected mid-stream, kill the request and re-issue it to a different model variant, a different seed, or a slightly re-phrased prompt. |
| **KV-cache deduplication** | If the model is about to generate a span it has already generated (detectable via cache hit), serve a cached *alternative* continuation from a prior divergent branch rather than the repeat. |

---

## Ranking

Two axes, so a 2-D table. **Effectiveness** = expected reduction in loop frequency *without* degrading answer quality. **Cost to test** = engineering effort + compute + evaluation time to get a signal.

| Rank | Strategy | Layer | Effectiveness | Cost to test | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sliding-window loop detector + forced continuation | Decoding | **High** | **Low** | A few hundred lines of code; evaluate on a held-out set of known-looping prompts. Highest ROI. |
| 2 | Adaptive token budget / early stop | Serving | **High** | **Low** | Truncates the damage; pairs naturally with #1. |
| 3 | Multi-attempt with diversity seeds | Serving | **High** | **Low–Med** | 2–3× latency/cost per request but zero model changes; very easy A/B test. |
| 4 | Streaming loop-detection middleware | Serving | **Med–High** | **Low** | Catches loops post-hoc; can't prevent them but limits user-visible damage. |
| 5 | Structured scaffold + "do not re-derive" prompt | Prompting | **Med** | **Very Low** | One-prompt change; easy to A/B. Modest effect alone, good as a baseline. |
| 6 | Adaptive n-gram penalty (trigger-based) | Sampling | **Med** | **Low** | Easy to wire into the sampler; risk of hurting legitimate re-use if threshold is wrong. |
| 7 | DPO on loop/non-loop pairs | Training | **Med–High** | **Med** | Needs a few thousand pairs but no RL infra. Can be done on a LoRA adapter. |
| 8 | SFT on curated non-looping traces | Training | **Med** | **Med** | Filtering + retraining; effect depends on how much of the SFT corpus was already loop-free. |
| 9 | Temperature annealing on loop trigger | Sampling | **Med** | **Low** | Cheap to try; effect is probabilistic and can occasionally degrade coherence. |
| 10 | Checkpoint-and-rollback | Decoding | **Med** | **Med** | KV-cache snapshotting is non-trivial in most inference stacks. |
| 11 | Best-of-n with loop filter | Decoding | **High** | **Med–High** | *n*× compute; great for offline/eval, expensive for interactive serving. |
| 12 | PRM with novelty signal | Training | **High** | **High** | Needs a labelled PRM; best long-term fix but weeks of work. |
| 13 | RL with repetition-shaped reward | Training | **High** | **High** | Most principled; requires RL infra and careful reward shaping to avoid reward hacking. |
| 14 | KV-cache deduplication | Serving | **Med** | **High** | Interesting but hard to implement cleanly in current serving stacks. |
| 15 | Distillation from non-looping oracle | Training | **Unknown** | **High** | Dependent on whether a suitable oracle exists; hard to evaluate. |
| 16 | Speculative-decode rejection | Sampling | **Low–Med** | **Med** | Only helps if you already run speculative decoding; marginal gain otherwise. |
| 17 | Periodic self-check injection | Prompting | **Low–Med** | **Very Low** | Cheap to try but the meta-prompt adds tokens and can itself become a loop. |
| 18 | Few-shot non-repetitive exemplars | Prompting | **Low** | **Very Low** | Nice-to-have; effect is small and context-length expensive. |
| 19 | Request re-routing | Serving | **Low–Med** | **Low** | Works as a last resort; doesn't fix the underlying tendency. |

### Practical takeaway

The **highest-leverage first move** is the combo of rows 1 + 2: a sliding-window loop detector that, on trigger, (a) injects a "proceed to the next step" nudge and (b) shrinks the remaining token budget to force a conclusion. Both are pure inference-time code, testable in a day on a handful of known-looping prompts, and together they eliminate most user-visible damage.

The **best long-term fix** is a PRM or RL objective that rewards *progress* (rows 12–13), because it shapes the model's native behaviour rather than papering over it at inference time. But it's weeks of work, so it's the second phase, not the first.

Prompting changes (rows 5, 17, 18) are worth having in the baseline as a free improvement, but none of them alone is sufficient—verbatim loops are a decoding-dynamics problem, not primarily an instruction-following one.
